La vida es sueño

Pedro Calderón de la Barca — EMOTHE0020_LaVidaEsSueno

Personas que hablan en ella

  • Segismundo, príncipe
  • Clotaldo, viejo
  • Estrella, infanta
  • Clarín, gracioso

NOTA - Los GUARDAS son los soldados que están en la torre custodiando a Segismundo. El texto solo habla de GUARDAS en el elenco, mientras que en el desarrollo de la obra se habla siempre de SOLDADOS, sea el caso que sea. Nosotros respetaremos externamente el texto en el que nos basamos -solo hablaremos de soldados-, pero internamente, en el XML-TEI, asociaremos los soldados de la torre a los GUARDAS y el resto de soldados a los SOLDADOS

Jornada I

Sale en lo alto de un monte Rosaura en hábito de hombre, de camino, y en representando los primeros versos va bajando.

Rosaura

1Hipogrifo violento,Silva
2que corriste parejas con el viento,
3¿dónde, rayo sin llama,
4pájaro sin matiz, pez sin escama
5y bruto sin instinto
6natural, al confuso laberinto
7de esas desnudas peñas
8te desbocas, te arrastras y despeñas?
9Quédate en este monte,
10donde tengan los brutos su Faetonte;
11que yo, sin más camino
12que el que me dan las leyes del destino,
13ciega y desesperada,
14bajaré la cabeza enmarañada
15deste monte eminente
16que abrasa al sol el ceño de la frente.
17Mal, Polonia, recibes
18a un estranjero, pues con sangre escribes
19su entrada en tus arenas;
20y apenas llega, cuando llega a penas.
21Bien mi suerte lo dice;
22mas ¿dónde halló piedad un infelice?

Sale Clarín, gracioso.

Clarín

23Di dos, y no me dejes
24en la posada a mí cuando te quejes;
25que si dos hemos sido
26los que de nuestra patria hemos salido
27a probar aventuras,
28dos los que entre desdichas y locuras
29aquí habemos llegado,
30y dos los que del monte hemos rodado,
31¿no es razón que yo sienta
32meterme en el pesar y no en la cuenta?

Rosaura

33No quise darte parte
34en mis quejas, Clarín, por no quitarte,
35llorando tu desvelo,
36el derecho que tienes al consuelo;
37que tanto gusto había
38en quejarse, un filósofo decía,
39que, a trueco de quejarse,
40habían las desdichas de buscarse.

Clarín

41El filósofo era
42un borracho barbón. ¡Oh, quién le diera
43más de mil bofetadas!
44Quejárase después de muy bien dadas.
45Mas ¿qué haremos, señora,
46a pie, solos, perdidos y a esta hora
47en un desierto monte,
48cuando se parte el sol a otro horizonte?

Rosaura

49¿Quién ha visto sucesos tan estraños?
50Mas si la vista no padece engaños
51que hace la fantasía,
52a la medrosa luz que aún tiene el día
53me parece que veo
54un edificio.

Clarín

un edificio. O miente mi deseo,
55o termino las señas.

Rosaura

56Rústico nace entre desnudas peñas
57un palacio tan breve
58que el sol apenas a mirar se atreve;
59con tan rudo artificio
60la arquitectura está de su edificio,
61que parece, a las plantas
62de tantas rocas y de peñas tantas
63que al sol tocan la lumbre,
64peñasco que ha rodado de la cumbre.

Clarín

65Vámonos acercando,
66que éste es mucho mirar, señora, cuando
67es mejor que la gente
68que habita en ella, generosamente
69nos admita.

Rosaura

nos admita. La puerta
70–mejor diré funesta boca– abierta
71está, y desde su centro
72nace la noche, pues la engendra dentro.

Suena ruido de cadenas.

82Clarín...

Clarín

Clarín

desta encantada torre. Yo aun no tengo

Rosaura

85¿No es breve luz aquella
86caduca exhalación, pálida estrella,
87que en trémulos desmayos,
88pulsando ardores y latiendo rayos,
89hace más tenebrosa
90la obscura habitación con luz dudosa?
91Sí, pues a sus reflejos
92puedo determinar –aunque de lejos–
93una prisión obscura
94que es de un vivo cadáver sepultura;
95y, porque más me asombre,
96en el traje de fiera yace un hombre
97de prisiones cargado
98y sólo de la luz acompañado.
99Pues huir no podemos,
100desde aquí sus desdichas escuchemos;
101sepamos lo que dice.

Descúbrese Segismundo con una cadena y la luz, vestido de pieles.

Segismundo

102¡Ay mísero de mí! Y ¡ay infelice!
103Apurar, cielos, pretendo,Décima
104ya que me tratáis así,
105qué delito cometí
106contra vosotros naciendo.
107Aunque si nací, ya entiendo
108qué delito he cometido:
109bastante causa ha tenido
110vuestra justicia y rigor,
111pues el delito mayor
112del hombre es haber nacido.
113Sólo quisiera saber,
114para apurar mis desvelos,
115–dejando a una parte, cielos,
116el delito de nacer–
117qué más os pude ofender,
118para castigarme más.
119¿No nacieron los demás?
120Pues si los demás nacieron,
121¿qué privilegios tuvieron
122que yo no gocé jamás?
123Nace el ave, y con las galas
124que le dan belleza suma,
125apenas es flor de pluma
126o ramillete con alas,
127cuando las etéreas salas
128corta con velocidad,
129negándose a la piedad
130del nido que deja en calma;
131¿y, teniendo yo más alma,
132tengo menos libertad?
133Nace el bruto, y con la piel
134que dibujan manchas bellas,
135apenas signo es de estrellas,
136gracias al docto pincel,
137cuando, atrevido y cruel,
138la humana necesidad
139le enseña a tener crueldad,
140monstruo de su laberinto;
141¿y yo, con mejor distinto,
142tengo menos libertad?
143Nace el pez, que no respira,
144aborto de ovas y lamas,
145y apenas, bajel de escamas,
146sobre las ondas se mira,
147cuando a todas partes gira,
148midiendo la inmensidad
149de tanta capacidad
150como le da el centro frío;
151¿y yo, con más albedrío,
152tengo menos libertad?
153Nace el arroyo, culebra
154que entre flores se desata,
155y apenas, sierpe de plata,
156entre las flores se quiebra,
157cuando músico celebra
158de las flores la piedad,
159que le dan la majestad,
160el campo abierto a su huida;
161¿y, teniendo yo más vida,
162tengo menos libertad?
163En llegando a esta pasión,
164un volcán, un Etna hecho,
165quisiera sacar del pecho
166pedazos del corazón.
167¿Qué ley, justicia o razón
168negar a los hombres sabe
169privilegio tan suave,
170excepción tan principal,
171que Dios le ha dado a un cristal,
172a un pez, a un bruto y a un ave?

Rosaura

173Temor y piedad en mí
174sus razones han causado.

Segismundo

180Pues la muerte te daré,

Rosaura

Segismundo

190Tu voz pudo enternecerme,
191tu presencia suspenderme
192y tu respeto turbarme.
193¿Quién eres? Que aunque yo aquí
194tan poco del mundo sé,
195que cuna y sepulcro fue
196esta torre para mí;
197y aunque desde que nací
198–si esto es nacer– sólo advierto
199este rústico desierto
200donde miserable vivo,
201siendo un esqueleto vivo,
202siendo un animado muerto;
203y aunque nunca vi ni hablé
204sino a un hombre solamente
205que aquí mis desdichas siente,
206por quien las noticias sé
207de cielo y tierra; y aunque
208aquí, porque más te asombres
209y monstruo humano me nombres,
210entre asombros y quimeras
211soy un hombre de las fieras
212y una fiera de los hombres;
213y aunque en desdichas tan graves
214la política he estudiado,
215de los brutos enseñado,
216advertido de las aves,
217y de los astros suaves
218los círculos he medido,
219tú, sólo tú, has suspendido
220la pasión a mis enojos,
221la suspensión a mis ojos,
222la admiración al oído.
223Con cada vez que te veo
224nueva admiración me das,
225y cuando te miro más,
226aún más mirarte deseo.
227Ojos hidrópicos creo
228que mis ojos deben ser,
229pues, cuando es muerte el beber,
230beben más, y desta suerte,
231viendo que el ver me da muerte,
232estoy muriendo por ver.
233Pero véate yo y muera;
234que no sé, rendido ya,
235si el verte muerte me da,
236el no verte qué me diera.
237Fuera más que muerte fiera,
238ira, rabia y dolor fuerte:
239fuera muerte; desta suerte
240su rigor he ponderado,
241pues dar vida a un desdichado
242es dar a un dichoso muerte.

Rosaura

243Con asombro de mirarte,
244con admiración de oírte,
245ni sé qué pueda decirte
246ni qué pueda preguntarte.
247Sólo diré que a esta parte
248hoy el cielo me ha guiado
249para haberme consolado,
250si consuelo puede ser,
251del que es desdichado, ver
252a otro que es más desdichado.
253Cuentan de un sabio que un día
254tan pobre y mísero estaba,
255que sólo se sustentaba
256de unas yerbas que comía.
257«¿Habrá otro —entre sí decía—
258más pobre y triste que yo?»
259Y cuando el rostro volvió,
260halló la respuesta, viendo
261que iba otro sabio cogiendo
262las hojas que él arrojó.
263Quejoso de la fortuna
264yo en este mundo vivía,
265y cuando entre mí decía:
266«¿Habrá otra persona alguna
267de suerte más importuna?»,
268piadoso me has respondido;
269pues, volviendo en mi sentido,
270hallo que las penas mías,
271para hacerlas tú alegrías,
272las hubieras recogido.
273Y por si acaso mis penasRomance
274pueden aliviarte en parte,
275óyelas atento, y toma
276las que dellas me sobraren.
277Yo soy...

296¡Oh vosotros, que, ignorantes,

su nombre es fuerza. ¿De qué

Clotaldo

395(¡Válgame el cielo! ¿Qué escucho?aparte
396Aún no sé determinarme
397si tales sucesos son
398ilusiones o verdades.
399Esta espada es la que yo
400dejé a la hermosa Violante,
401por señas que el que ceñida
402la trujera, había de hallarme
403amoroso como hijo
404y piadoso como padre.
405Pues ¿qué he de hacer, ¡ay de mí!,
406en confusión semejante,
407si quien la trae por favor
408para su muerte la trae,
409pues que sentenciado a muerte
410llega a mis pies? ¡Qué notable
411confusión! ¡Qué triste hado!
412¡Qué suerte tan inconstante!
413Éste es mi hijo, y las señas
414dicen bien con las señales
415del corazón, que por verle
416llama al pecho y en él bate
417las alas, y no pudiendo
418romper los candados, hace
419lo que aquel que está encerrado,
420y oyendo ruido en la calle
421se arroja por la ventana;
422y él así, como no sabe
423lo que pasa y oye el ruido,
424va a los ojos a asomarse,
425que son ventanas del pecho,
426por donde en lágrimas sale.
427¿Qué he de hacer? ¡Válgame el cielo!
428¿Qué he de hacer? Porque llevarle
429al Rey es llevarle, ¡ay, triste!
430a morir, pues ocultarle
431al Rey no puedo, conforme
432a la ley del homenaje.
433De una parte el amor propio,
434y la lealtad de otra parte,
435me rinden. Pero ¿qué dudo?
436¿La lealtad del Rey no es antes
437que la vida y que el honor?
438Pues ella viva y él falte.
439Fuera de que, si ahora atiendo
440a que dijo que a vengarse
441viene de un agravio, hombre
442que está agraviado es infame.
443No es mi hijo, no es mi hijo,
444ni tiene mi noble sangre.
445Pero si ya ha sucedido
446un peligro, de quien nadie
447se libró, porque el honor
448es de materia tan fácil
449que con una acción se quiebra
450o se mancha con un aire,
451¿qué más puede hacer, qué más,
452el que es noble, de su parte,
453que a costa de tantos riesgos
454haber venido a buscarle?
455Mi hijo es, mi sangre tiene,
456pues tiene valor tan grande.
457Y así, entre una y otra duda,
458el medio más importante
459es irme al Rey y decirle
460que es mi hijo, y que le mate.
461Quizá la misma piedad
462de mi honor podrá obligarle;
463y si le merezco vivo,
464yo le ayudaré a vengarse
465de su agravio. Mas si el Rey,
466en sus rigores constante,
467le da muerte, morirá
468sin saber que soy su padre.)
469Venid conmigo, estranjeros.
470No temáis, no, de que os falte
471compañía en las desdichas;
472pues en duda semejante
473de vivir o de morir,
474no sé cuáles son más grandes.

540Vos alegáis que habéis sido
541hija de hermana mayor;
542yo, que varón he nacido

Basilio

589Sobrinos, dadme los brazos,
590y creed, pues que leales
591a mi precepto amoroso
592venís con afectos tales,
593que a nadie deje quejoso
594y los dos quedéis iguales.
595Y así, cuando me confieso
596rendido al prolijo peso,
597sólo os pido en la ocasión
598silencio, que admiración
599ha de pedirla el suceso.
600Ya sabéis –estadme atentosRomance
601amados sobrinos míos,
602corte ilustre de Polonia,
603vasallos, deudos y amigos–
604ya sabéis que yo en el mundo
605por mi ciencia he merecido
606el sobrenombre de docto;
607pues, contra el tiempo y olvido,
608los pinceles de Timantes,
609los mármoles de Lisipo,
610en el ámbito del orbe
611me aclaman el gran Basilio.
612Ya sabéis que son las ciencias
613que más curso y más estimo
614matemáticas sutiles,
615por quien al tiempo le quito,
616por quien a la fama rompo
617la juridición y oficio
618de enseñar más cada día;
619pues, cuando en mis tablas miro
620presentes las novedades
621de los venideros siglos,
622le gano al tiempo las gracias
623de contar lo que yo he dicho.
624Esos círculos de nieve,
625esos doseles de vidrio,
626que el sol ilumina a rayos,
627que parte la luna a giros,
628esos orbes de diamantes,
629esos globos cristalinos,
630que las estrellas adornan
631y que campean los signos,
632son el estudio mayor
633de mis años, son los libros
634donde, en papel de diamante,
635en cuadernos de zafiros,
636escribe con líneas de oro,
637en caracteres distintos,
638el cielo nuestros sucesos
639ya adversos o ya benignos.
640Éstos leo tan veloz
641que con mi espíritu sigo
642sus rápidos movimientos
643por rumbos y por caminos.
644¡Pluguiera al cielo, primero
645que mi ingenio hubiera sido
646de sus márgenes comento
647y de sus hojas registro,
648hubiera sido mi vida
649el primero desperdicio
650de sus iras, y que en ellas
651mi tragedia hubiera sido!
652Porque de los infelices
653aun el mérito es cuchillo;
654que a quien le daña el saber
655homicida es de sí mismo.
656Dígalo yo, aunque mejor
657lo dirán sucesos míos,
658para cuya admiración
659otra vez silencio os pido.
660En Clorilene, mi esposa,
661tuve un infelice hijo,
662en cuyo parto los cielos
663se agotaron de prodigios,
664antes que a la luz hermosa
665le diese el sepulcro vivo
666de un vientre, porque el nacer
667y el morir son parecidos.
668Su madre infinitas veces,
669entre ideas y delirios
670del sueño, vio que rompía
671sus entrañas, atrevido,
672un monstruo en forma de hombre,
673y entre su sangre teñido
674le daba muerte naciendo,
675víbora humana del siglo.
676Llegó de su parto el día,
677y los presagios cumplidos
678–porque tarde o nunca son
679mentirosos los impíos–,
680nació en horóscopo tal
681que el sol, en su sangre tinto,
682entraba sañudamente
683con la luna en desafío;
684y, siendo valla la tierra,
685los dos faroles divinos
686a luz entera luchaban,
687ya que no a brazo partido.
688El mayor, el más horrendo
689eclipse que ha padecido
690el sol después que con sangre
691lloró la muerte de Cristo,
692éste fue, porque, anegado
693el orbe entre incendios vivos,
694presumió que padecía
695el último parasismo.
696Los cielos se escurecieron,
697temblaron los edificios,
698llovieron piedras las nubes,
699corrieron sangre los ríos.
700En este mísero, en este
701mortal planeta o signo
702nació Segismundo, dando
703de su condición indicios
704pues dio la muerte a su madre;
705con cuya fiereza dijo:
706«Hombre soy, pues que ya empiezo
707a pagar mal beneficios».
708Yo, acudiendo a mis estudios,
709en ellos y en todo miro
710que Segismundo sería
711el hombre más atrevido,
712el príncipe más cruel
713y el monarca más impío,
714por quien su reino vendría
715a ser parcial y diviso,
716escuela de las traiciones
717y academia de los vicios;
718y él, de su furor llevado,
719entre asombros y delitos,
720había de poner en mí
721las plantas, y yo rendido
722a sus pies me había de ver
723–¡con qué congoja lo digo!–,
724siendo alfombra de sus plantas
725las canas del rostro mío.
726¿Quién no da crédito al daño,
727y más al daño que ha visto
728en su estudio, donde hace
729el amor propio su oficio?
730Pues, dando crédito yo
731a los hados, que adivinos
732me pronosticaban daños
733en fatales vaticinios,
734determiné de encerrar
735la fiera que había nacido,
736por ver si el sabio tenía
737en las estrellas dominio.
738Publicose que el Infante
739nació muerto; y, prevenido,
740hice labrar una torre
741entre las peñas y riscos
742desos montes, donde apenas
743la luz ha hallado camino,
744por defenderle la entrada
745sus rústicos obeliscos.
746Las graves penas y leyes,
747que con públicos editos
748declararon que ninguno
749entrase a un vedado sitio
750del monte, se ocasionaron
751de las causas que os he dicho.
752Allí Segismundo vive
753mísero, pobre y cautivo,
754adonde solo Clotaldo
755le ha hablado, tratado y visto.
756Éste le ha enseñado ciencias;
757éste en la ley le ha instruido
758católica, siendo solo
759de sus miserias testigo.
760Aquí hay tres cosas: la una
761que yo, Polonia, os estimo
762tanto que os quiero librar
763de la opresión y servicio
764de un rey tirano, porqué
765no fuera señor benigno
766el que a su patria y su imperio
767pusiera en tanto peligro.
768La otra es considerar
769que, si a mi sangre le quito
770el derecho que le dieron
771humano fuero y divino,
772no es cristiana caridad;
773pues ninguna ley ha dicho
774que, por reservar yo a otro
775de tirano y de atrevido,
776pueda yo serlo, supuesto
777que, si es tirano mi hijo,
778porque él delitos no haga
779vengo yo a hacer los delitos.
780Es la última y tercera
781el ver cuánto yerro ha sido
782dar crédito fácilmente
783a los sucesos previstos;
784pues, aunque su inclinación
785le dicte sus precipicios,
786quizá no le vencerán,
787porque el hado más esquivo,
788la inclinación más violenta,
789el planeta más impío,
790sólo el albedrío inclinan,
791no fuerzan el albedrío.
792Y así, entre una y otra causa
793vacilante y discursivo,
794previne un remedio tal
795que os suspenda los sentidos:
796yo he de ponerle mañana,
797sin que él sepa que es mi hijo
798y rey vuestro, a Segismundo
799–que aqueste su nombre ha sido–
800en mi dosel, en mi silla,
801y, en fin, en el lugar mío,
802donde os gobierne y os mande
803y donde todos rendidos
804la obediencia le juréis;
805pues con aquesto consigo
806tres cosas, con que respondo
807a las otras tres que he dicho.
808Es la primera, que siendo
809prudente, cuerdo y benigno,
810desmintiendo en todo al hado
811que dél tantas cosas dijo,
812gozaréis el natural
813príncipe vuestro, que ha sido
814cortesano de unos montes
815y de sus fieras vecino.
816Es la segunda, que si él,
817soberbio, osado, atrevido
818y cruel, con rienda suelta
819corre el campo de sus vicios,
820habré yo piadoso entonces
821con mi obligación cumplido;
822y luego en desposeerle
823haré como rey invicto,
824siendo el volverle a la cárcel
825no crueldad, sino castigo.
826Es la tercera, que siendo
827el príncipe como os digo,
828por lo que os amo, vasallos,
829os daré reyes más dignos
830de la corona y el cetro,
831pues serán mis dos sobrinos;
832juntando en uno el derecho
833de los dos, y convenidos
834con la fe del matrimonio,
835tendrán lo que han merecido.
836Esto como rey os mando,
837esto como padre os pido,
838esto como sabio os ruego,
839esto como anciano os digo;
840y si el Séneca español,
841que era humilde esclavo, dijo,
842de su república un rey,
843como esclavo os lo suplico.

989Fue, señor, desta manera.

996así el humano discurso

1018Dejando aparte el dudar

1020pues que ya queda probado

1041en las regiones supremas

1044Encarecí el vuelo altivo,

1048Él no hubo menester más,

1059mis desdichas me consuelan,
1060pues, por lo menos, si estoy

Los GUARDAS son los soldados que están en la torre custodiando a Segismundo. El texto solo habla de GUARDAS en el elenco, mientras que en el desarrollo de la obra se habla siempre de SOLDADOS, sea el caso que sea. Nosotros respetaremos externamente el texto en el que nos basamos -solo hablaremos de soldados-, pero internamente, en el XML-TEI, asociaremos los soldados de la torre a los GUARDAS y el resto de soldados a los SOLDADOS

Act I

At one side a craggy mountain, at the other a tower, the lower part of which serves as the prison of Sigismund. The door facing the spectators is half open. The action commences at nightfall.

SCENE I.

ROSAURA, CLARIN.

ROSAURA in man's attire appears on the rocky heights and descends to the plain. She is followed by CLARIN.

ROSAURA.

1Wild hippogriff swift speeding,
2Thou that dost run, the winged winds exceeding,
3Bolt which no flash illumes,
4Fish without scales, bird without shifting plumes,
5And brute awhile bereft
6Of natural instinct, why to this wild cleft,
7This labyrinth of naked rocks, dost sweep
8Unreined, uncurbed, to plunge thee down the steep?
9Stay in this mountain wold,
10And let the beasts their Phaeton behold.
11For I, without a guide,
12Save what the laws of destiny decide,
13Benighted, desperate, blind.
14Take any path whatever that doth wind
15Down this rough mountain to its base,
16Whose wrinkled brow in heaven frowns in the sun's bright face.
17Ah, Poland! in ill mood
18Hast thou received a stranger, since in blood
19The name thou writest on thy sands
20Of her who hardly here fares hardly at thy hands.
21My fate may well say so:—
22But where shall one poor wretch find pity in her woe?

CLARIN.

23Say two, if you please;
24Don't leave me out when making plaints like these.
25For if we are the two
26Who left our native country with the view
27Of seeking strange adventures, if we be
28The two who, madly and in misery,
29Have got so far as this, and if we still
30Are the same two who tumbled down this hill,
31Does it not plainly to a wrong amount,
32To put me in the pain and not in the account?

ROSAURA.

33I do not wish to impart,

36Of making for thyself thy lamentation;
37For there is such a pleasure in complaining,
38That a philosopher I've heard maintaining
39One ought to seek a sorrow and be vain of it,
40In order to be privileged to complain of it.

41That same philosopher
42Was an old drunken fool, unless I err:
43Oh, that I could a thousand thumps present him,
44In order for complaining to content him!
45But what, my lady, say,
46Are we to do, on foot, alone, our way
47Lost in the shades of night?
48For see, the sun descends another sphere to light.

ROSAURA.

49So strange a misadventure who has seen?
50But if my sight deceives me not, between
51These rugged rocks, half-lit by the moon's ray
52And the declining day,
53It seems, or is it fancy? that I see
54A human dwelling?

CLARIN.

55So it seems to me,
56Unless my wish the longed-for lodging mocks.

ROSAURA.

57A rustic little palace 'mid the rocks
58Uplifts its lowly roof,
59Scarce seen by the far sun that shines aloof.
60Of such a rude device
61Is the whole structure of this edifice,
62That lying at the feet
63Of these gigantic crags that rise to greet
64The sun's first beams of gold,
65It seems a rock that down the mountain rolled.

CLARIN.

66Let us approach more near,
67For long enough we've looked at it from here;
68Then better we shall see
69If those who dwell therein will generously
70A welcome give us.

ROSAURA.

71See an open door
72(Funereal mouth 'twere best the name it bore),
73From which as from a womb
74The night is born, engendered in its gloom.

[The sound of chains is heard within.]

CLARIN.

75Heavens! what is this I hear?

ROSAURA.

76Half ice, half fire, I stand transfixed with fear.

CLARIN.

77A sound of chains, is it not?
78Some galley-slave his sentence here hath got;
79My fear may well suggest it so may be.

SCENE II.

SIGISMUND, [in the tower.] ROSAURA, CLARIN.

SIGISMUND.

80[within]. Alas! Ah, wretched me! Ah, wretched me!

ROSAURA.

81Oh what a mournful wail!
82Again my pains, again my fears prevail.

CLARIN.

83Again with fear I die.

ROSAURA.

84Clarin!

CLARIN.

85My lady!

ROSAURA.

86Let us turn and fly
87The risks of this enchanted tower.

CLARIN.

88For one,
89I scarce have strength to stand, much less to run.

ROSAURA.

90Is not that glimmer there afar —
91That dying exhalation — that pale star —
92A tiny taper, which, with trembling blaze
93Flickering 'twixt struggling flames and dying rays,
94With ineffectual spark
95Makes the dark dwelling place appear more dark?
96Yes, for its distant light,
97Reflected dimly, brings before my sight
98A dungeon's awful gloom,
99Say rather of a living corse, a living tomb;
100And to increase my terror and surprise,
101Drest in the skins of beasts a man there lies:
102A piteous sight,
103Chained, and his sole companion this poor light.
104Since then we cannot fly,
105Let us attentive to his words draw nigh,
106Whatever they may be.

[The doors of the tower open wide, and SIGISMUND is discovered in chains and clad in the skins of beasts. The light in the tower increases.]

SIGISMUND.

107Alas! Ah, wretched me! Ah, wretched me!
108Heaven, here lying all forlorn,
109I desire from thee to know,
110Since thou thus dost treat me so,
111Why have I provoked thy scorn
112By the crime of being born?—
113Though for being born I feel
114Heaven with me must harshly deal,
115Since man's greatest crime on earth
116Is the fatal fact of birth —
117Sin supreme without appeal.
118This alone I ponder o'er,
119My strange mystery to pierce through;
120Leaving wholly out of view
121Germs my hapless birthday bore,
122How have I offended more,
123That the more you punish me?
124Must not other creatures be
125Born? If born, what privilege
126Can they over me allege
127Of which I should not be free?
128Birds are born, the bird that sings,
129Richly robed by Nature's dower,
130Scarcely floats — a feathered flower,
131Or a bunch of blooms with wings —
132When to heaven's high halls it springs,
133Cuts the blue air fast and free,
134And no longer bound will be
135By the nest's secure control:—
136And with so much more of soul,
137Must I have less liberty?
138Beasts are born, the beast whose skin
139Dappled o'er with beauteous spots,
140As when the great pencil dots
141Heaven with stars, doth scarce begin
142From its impulses within—
143Nature's stern necessity,
144To be schooled in cruelty,—
145Monster, waging ruthless war:—
146And with instincts better far
147Must I have less liberty?
148Fish are born, the spawn that breeds
149Where the oozy sea-weeds float,
150Scarce perceives itself a boat,
151Scaled and plated for its needs,
152When from wave to wave it speeds,
153Measuring all the mighty sea,
154Testing its profundity
155To its depths so dark and chill:—
156And with so much freer will,
157Must I have less liberty?
158Streams are born, a coiled-up snake
159When its path the streamlet finds,
160Scarce a silver serpent winds
161'Mong the flowers it must forsake,
162But a song of praise doth wake,
163Mournful though its music be,
164To the plain that courteously
165Opes a path through which it flies:—
166And with life that never dies,
167Must I have less liberty?
168When I think of this I start,
169Aetna-like in wild unrest
170I would pluck from out my breast
171Bit by bit my burning heart:—
172For what law can so depart
173From all right, as to deny
174One lone man that liberty —
175That sweet gift which God bestows
176On the crystal stream that flows,
177Birds and fish that float or fly?

ROSAURA.

178Fear and deepest sympathy
179Do I feel at every word.

SIGISMUND.

180Who my sad lament has heard?
181What! Clotaldo!

CLARIN

182[aside to his mistress]. Say 'tis he.aparte

ROSAURA.

183No, 'tis but a wretch (ah, me!)
184Who in these dark caves and cold
185Hears the tale your lips unfold.

SIGISMUND.

186Then you'll die for listening so,
187That you may not know I know
188That you know the tale I told.

[Seizes her.]

189Yes, you'll die for loitering near:
190In these strong arms gaunt and grim
191I will tear you limb from limb.

CLARIN.

192I am deaf and couldn't hear:—
193No!

ROSAURA.

194If human heart you bear,
195'Tis enough that I prostrate me.
196At thy feet, to liberate me!

SIGISMUND.

197Strange thy voice can so unbend me,
198Strange thy sight can so suspend me,
199And respect so penetrate me!
200Who art thou? for though I see
201Little from this lonely room,
202This, my cradle and my tomb.
203Being all the world to me,
204And if birthday it could be,
205Since my birthday I have known
206But this desert wild and lone,
207Where throughout my life's sad course
208I have lived, a breathing corse,
209I have moved, a skeleton;
210And though I address or see
211Never but one man alone,
212Who my sorrows all hath known,
213And through whom have come to me
214Notions of earth, sky, and sea;
215And though harrowing thee again,
216Since thou'lt call me in this den,
217Monster fit for bestial feasts,
218I'm a man among wild beasts,
219And a wild beast amongst men.
220But though round me has been wrought
221All this woe, from beasts I've learned
222Polity, the same discerned
223Heeding what the birds had taught,
224And have measured in my thought
225The fair orbits of the spheres;
226You alone, 'midst doubts and fears,
227Wake my wonder and surprise —
228Give amazement to my eyes,
229Admiration to my ears.
230Every time your face I see
231You produce a new amaze:
232After the most steadfast gaze,
233I again would gazer be.
234I believe some hydropsy
235Must affect my sight, I think
236Death must hover on the brink
237Of those wells of light, your eyes,
238For I look with fresh surprise,
239And though death result, I drink.
240Let me see and die: forgive me;
241For I do not know, in faith,
242If to see you gives me death,
243What to see you not would give me;
244Something worse than death would grieve me,
245Anger, rage, corroding care,
246Death, but double death it were,
247Death with tenfold terrors rife,
248Since what gives the wretched life,
249Gives the happy death, despair!

ROSAURA.

250Thee to see wakes such dismay,
251Thee to hear I so admire,
252That I'm powerless to inquire,
253That I know not what to say:
254Only this, that I to-day,
255Guided by a wiser will,
256Have here come to cure my ill,
257Here consoled my grief to see,
258If a wretch consoled can be
259Seeing one more wretched still.
260Of a sage, who roamed dejected,
261Poor, and wretched, it is said,
262That one day, his wants being fed
263By the herbs which he collected,
264"Is there one" (he thus reflected)
265"Poorer than I am to-day?"
266Turning round him to survey,
267He his answer got, detecting
268A still poorer sage collecting
269Even the leaves he threw away.
270Thus complaining to excess,
271Mourning fate, my life I led,
272And when thoughtlessly I said
273To myself, "Does earth possess
274One more steeped in wretchedness?"
275I in thee the answer find.
276Since revolving in my mind,
277I perceive that all my pains
278To become thy joyful gains
279Thou hast gathered and entwined.
280And if haply some slight solace
281By these pains may be imparted,
282Hear attentively the story
283Of my life's supreme disasters.
284I am ….

SCENE III.

CLOTALDO, Soldiers, SIGISMUND, ROSAURA, CLARIN.

CLOTALDO.

285[within]. Warders of this tower,
286Who, or sleeping or faint-hearted,
287Give an entrance to two persons
288Who herein have burst a passage . . . .

ROSAURA.

289New confusion now I suffer.

SIGISMUND.

290'Tis Clotaldo, who here guards me;
291Are not yet my miseries ended?

CLOTALDO.

292[within]. Hasten hither, quick! be active!
293And before they can defend them,
294Kill them on the spot, or capture!

[ALL]

295[Voices within.] Treason!

CLARIN.

296Watchguards of this tower,
297Who politely let us pass here,
298Since you have the choice of killing
299Or of capturing, choose the latter.

[Enter CLOTALDO and Soldiers; he with a pistol, and all with their faces covered.]

CLOTALDO.

300[aside to the Soldiers]. Keep your faces all well covered,aparte
301For it is a vital matter
302That we should be known by no one,
303While I question these two stragglers.aparte

CLARIN.

304Are there masqueraders here?

CLOTALDO.

305Ye who in your ignorant rashness
306Have passed through the bounds and limits
307Of this interdicted valley,
308'Gainst the edict of the King,
309Who has publicly commanded
310None should dare descry the wonder
311That among these rocks is guarded,
312Yield at once your arms and lives,
313Or this pistol, this cold aspic
314Formed of steel, the penetrating
315Poison of two balls will scatter,
316The report and fire of which
317Will the air astound and startle.

SIGISMUND.

318Ere you wound them, ere you hurt them,
319Will my life, O tyrant master,
320Be the miserable victim
321Of these wretched chains that clasp me;
322Since in them, I vow to God,
323I will tear myself to fragments
324With my hands, and with my teeth,
325In these rocks here, in these caverns,
326Ere I yield to their misfortunes,
327Or lament their sad disaster.

CLOTALDO.

328If you know that your misfortunes,
329Sigismund, are unexampled,
330Since before being born you died
331By Heaven's mystical enactment;
332If you know these fetters are
333Of your furies oft so rampant
334But the bridle that detains them,
335But the circle that contracts them.
336Why these idle boasts? The door
337[To the Soldiers.] Of this narrow prison fasten;
338Leave him there secured.

SIGISMUND.

339Ah, heavens,
340It is wise of you to snatch me
341Thus from freedom! since my rage
342'Gainst you had become Titanic,
343Since to break the glass and crystal
344Gold-gates of the sun, my anger
345On the firm-fixed rocks' foundations
346Would have mountains piled of marble.

CLOTALDO.

347'Tis that you should not so pile them
348That perhaps these ills have happened,

[Some of the SOLDIERS lead SIGISMUND into his prison, the doors of which are closed upon him.]

SCENE IV.

ROSAURA, CLOTALDO, CLARIN, Soldiers.

ROSAURA.

349Since I now have seen how pride
350Can offend thee, I were hardened
351Sure in folly not here humbly
352At thy feet for life to ask thee;
353Then to me extend thy pity,
354Since it were a special harshness
355If humility and pride,
356Both alike were disregarded.

CLARIN.

357If Humility and Pride
358Those two figures who have acted
359Many and many a thousand times
360In the "autos sacramentales",
361Do not move you, I, who am neither
362Proud nor humble, but a sandwich
363Partly mixed of both, entreat you
364To extend to us your pardon.

CLOTALDO.

365Ho!

SOLDIERS.

366My lord?

CLOTALDO.

367Disarm the two,
368And their eyes securely bandage,
369So that they may not be able
370To see whither they are carried.

ROSAURA.

371This is, sir, my sword; to thee
372Only would I wish to hand it,
373Since in fine of all the others
374Thou art chief, and I could hardly
375Yield it unto one less noble.

CLARIN.

376Mine I'll give the greatest rascal
377Of your troop: [To a Soldier.] so take it, you.

ROSAURA.

378And if I must die, to thank thee
379For thy pity, I would leave thee
380This as pledge, which has its value
381From the owner who once wore it;
382That thou guard it well, I charge thee,
383For although I do not know
384What strange secret it may carry,
385This I know, that some great mystery
386Lies within this golden scabbard,
387Since relying but on it
388I to Poland here have travelled
389To revenge a wrong.

CLOTALDO

390[aside.] Just heavens!aparte
391What is this? Still graver, darker,
392Grow my doubts and my confusion,
393My anxieties and my anguish. —
394Speak, who gave you this?

ROSAURA.

395A woman.

CLOTALDO.

396And her name?

ROSAURA.

397To that my answer
398Must be silence.

CLOTALDO.

399But from what
400Do you now infer, or fancy,
401That this sword involves a secret?

ROSAURA.

402She who gave it said: "Depart hence
403Into Poland, and by study,
404Stratagem, and skill so manage
405That this sword may be inspected
406By the nobles and the magnates
407Of that land, for you, I know,
408Will by one of them be guarded,"—
409But his name, lest he was dead,
410Was not then to me imparted.

CLOTALDO

411[aside]. Bless me, Heaven! what's this I hear?aparte
412For so strangely has this happened,
413That I cannot yet determine
414If 'tis real or imagined.
415This is the same sword that I
416Left with beauteous Violante,
417As a pledge unto its wearer,
418Who might seek me out thereafter,
419As a son that I would love him,
420And protect him as a father.
421What is to be done (ah, me!)
422In confusion so entangled,
423If he who for safety bore it
424Bears it now but to dispatch him,
425Since condemned to death he cometh
426To my feet? How strange a marvel!
427What a lamentable fortune!
428How unstable! how unhappy!
429This must be my son — the tokens
430All declare it, superadded
431To the flutter of the heart,
432That to see him loudly rappeth
433At the breast, and not being able
434With its throbs to burst its chamber,
435Does as one in prison, who,
436Hearing tumult in the alley,
437Strives to look from out the window;
438Thus, not knowing what here passes
439Save the noise, the heart uprusheth
440To the eyes the cause to examine —
441They the windows of the heart,
442Out through which in tears it glances.
443What is to be done? (O Heavens!)
444What is to be done? To drag him
445Now before the King were death;
446But to hide him from my master,
447That I cannot do, according
448To my duty as a vassal.
449Thus my loyalty and self-love
450Upon either side attack me;
451Each would win. But wherefore doubt?
452Is not loyalty a grander,
453Nobler thing than life, than honour?
454Then let loyalty live, no matter
455That he die; besides, he told me,
456If I well recall his language,
457That he came to revenge a wrong,
458But a wronged man is a lazar,—
459No, he cannot be my son,
460Not the son of noble fathers.
461But if some great chance, which no one
462Can be free from, should have happened,
463Since the delicate sense of honour
464Is a thing so fine, so fragile,
465That the slightest touch may break it,
466Or the faintest breath may tarnish,
467What could he do more, do more,
468He whose cheek the blue blood mantles,
469But at many risks to have come here
470It again to re-establish?
471Yes, he is my son, my blood,
472Since he shows himself so manly.
473And thus then betwixt two doubts
474A mid course alone is granted:
475'Tis to seek the King, and tell him
476Who he is, let what will happen.
477A desire to save my honour
478May appease my royal master;
479Should he spare his life, I then
480Will assist him in demanding
481His revenge; but if the King
482Should, persisting in his anger,
483Give him death, then he will die
484Without knowing I'm his father. —
485[To ROSAURA and CLARIN.] Come, then, come then with me, strangers.
486Do not fear in your disasters
487That you will not have companions
488In misfortune; for so balanced
489Are the gains of life or death,
490That I know not which are larger.

[Exeunt.]

SCENE V.

A HALL IN THE ROYAL PALACE.

[Enter at one side ASTOLFO and Soldiers, and at the other the INFANTA ESTRELLA and her Ladies. Military music and salutes within.]

ASTOLFO.

491Struck at once with admiration
492At thy starry eyes outshining,
493Mingle many a salutation,
494Drums and trumpet-notes combining,
495Founts and birds in alternation;
496Wondering here to see thee pass,
497Music in grand chorus gathers
498All her notes from grove and grass:
499Here are trumpets formed of feathers,
500There are birds that breathe in brass.
501All salute thee, fair Senora,
502Ordnance as their Queen proclaim thee,
503Beauteous birds as their Aurora,
504As their Pallas trumpets name thee,
505And the sweet flowers as their Flora;
506For Aurora sure thou art,
507Bright as day that conquers night —
508Thine is Flora's peaceful part,
509Thou art Pallas in thy might,
510And as Queen thou rul'st my heart.

ESTRELLA.

511If the human voice obeying
512Should with human action pair,
513Then you have said ill in saying
514All these flattering words and fair,
515Since in truth they are gainsaying
516This parade of victory,
517'Gainst which I my standard rear,
518Since they say, it seems to me,
519Not the flatteries that I hear,
520But the rigours that I see.
521Think, too, what a base invention
522From a wild beast's treachery sprung,—
523Fraudful mother of dissension —
524Is to flatter with the tongue,
525And to kill with the intention.

ASTOLFO.

526Ill informed you must have been,
527Fair Estrella, thus to throw
528Doubt on my respectful mien:
529Let your ear attentive lean
530While the cause I strive show.
531King Eustorgius the Fair,
532Third so called, died leaving two
533Daughters, and Basilius heir;
534Of his sisters I and you
535Are the children — I forbear
536To recall a single scene
537Save what's needful. Clorilene,
538Your good mother and my aunt,
539Who is now a habitant
540Of a sphere of sunnier sheen,
541Was the elder, of whom you
542Are the daughter; Recisunda,
543Whom God guard a thousand years,
544Her fair sister (Rosamunda
545Were she called if names were true)
546Wed in Muscovy, of whom
547I was born. 'Tis needful now
548The commencement to resume.
549King Basilius, who doth bow
550'Neath the weight of years, the doom
551Age imposes, more inclined
552To the studies of the mind
553Than to women, wifeless, lone,
554Without sons, to fill his throne
555I and you our way would find.
556You, the elder's child, averred,
557That the crown you stood more nigh:
558I, maintaining that you erred,
559Held, though born of the younger, I,
560Being a man, should be preferred.
561Thus our mutual pretension
562To our uncle we related,
563Who replied that he would mention
564Here, and on this day he stated,
565What might settle the dissension.
566With this end, from Muscovy
567I set out, and with that view,
568I to-day fair Poland see,
569And not making war on you,
570Wait till war you make on me.
571Would to love — that God so wise —
572That the crowd may be a sure
573Astrologue to read the skies,
574And this festive truce secure
575Both to you and me the prize,
576Making you a Queen, but Queen
577By my will, our uncle leaving
578You the throne we'll share between —
579And my love a realm receiving
580Dearer than a King's demesne.

ESTRELLA.

581Well, I must be generous too,
582For a gallantry so fine;
583This imperial realm you view,
584If I wish it to be mine
585'Tis to give it unto you.
586Though if I the truth confessed,
587I must fear your love may fail —
588Flattering words are words at best,
589For perhaps a truer tale
590Tells that portrait on your breast.

ASTOLFO.

591On that point complete content
592Will I give your mind, not here,
593For each sounding instrument
594[Drums are heard.] Tells us that the King is near,
595With his Court and Parliament.

SCENE VI.

The KING BASILIUS, with his retinue. —ASTOLFO, ESTRELLA, Ladies, Soldiers.

ESTRELLA.

596Learned Euclid . . .

ASTOLFO.

597Thales wise . .

ESTRELLA.

598The vast Zodiac . . .

ASTOLFO.

599The star spaces . . .

ESTRELLA.

600Who dost soar to . . .

ASTOLFO.

601Who dost rise…

ESTRELLA.

602The sun's orbit . . .

ASTOLFO.

603The stars' places . . .

ESTRELLA.

604To describe . . .

ASTOLFO.

605To map the skies . . .

ESTRELLA.

606Let me humbly interlacing . . .

ASTOLFO.

607Let me lovingly embracing . . .

ESTRELLA.

608Be the tendril of thy tree.

ASTOLFO.

609Bend respectfully my knee.

BASILIUS.

610Children, that dear word displacing
611Colder names, my arms here bless;
612And be sure, since you assented
613To my plan, my love's excess
614Will leave neither discontented,
615Or give either more or less.
616And though I from being old
617Slowly may the facts unfold,
618Hear in silence my narration,
619Keep reserved your admiration,
620Till the wondrous tale is told.
621You already know — I pray you
622Be attentive, dearest children,
623Great, illustrious Court of Poland,
624Faithful vassals, friends and kinsmen,
625You already know — my studies
626Have throughout the whole world given me
627The high title of "the learned,"
628Since 'gainst time and time's oblivion
629The rich pencils of Timanthes,
630The bright marbles of Lysippus,
631Universally proclaim me
632Through earth's bounds the great Basilius.
633You already know the sciences
634That I feel my mind most given to
635Are the subtle mathematics,
636By whose means my clear prevision
637Takes from rumour its slow office,
638Takes from time its jurisdiction
639Of, each day, new facts disclosing;
640Since in algebraic symbols
641When the fate of future ages
642On my tablets I see written,
643I anticipate time in telling
644What my science hath predicted.
645All those circles of pure snow,
646All those canopies of crystal,
647Which the sun with rays illumines,
648Which the moon cuts in its circles,
649All those orbs of twinkling diamond,
650All those crystal globes that glisten,
651All that azure field of stars
652Where the zodiac signs are pictured,
653Are the study of my life,
654Are the books where heaven has written
655Upon diamond-dotted paper,
656Upon leaves by sapphires tinted,
657With light luminous lines of gold,
658In clear characters distinctly
659All the events of human life,
660Whether adverse or benignant.
661These so rapidly I read
662That I follow with the quickness
663Of my thoughts the swiftest movements
664Of their orbits and their circles.
665Would to heaven, that ere my mind
666To those mystic books addicted
667Was the comment of their margins
668And of all their leaves the index,
669Would to heaven, I say, my life
670Had been offered the first victim
671Of its anger, that my death-stroke
672Had in this way have been given me,
673Since the unhappy find even merit
674Is the fatal knife that kills them,
675And his own self-murderer
676Is the man whom knowledge injures!—
677I may say so, but my story
678So will say with more distinctness,
679And to win your admiration
680Once again I pray you listen.—
681Clorilene, my wife, a son
682Bore me, so by fate afflicted
683That on his unhappy birthday
684All Heaven's prodigies assisted.
685Nay, ere yet to life's sweet life
686Gave him forth her womb, that living
687Sepulchre (for death and life
688Have like ending and beginning),
689Many a time his mother saw
690In her dreams' delirious dimness
691From her side a monster break,
692Fashioned like a man, but sprinkled
693With her blood, who gave her death,
694By that human viper bitten.
695Round his birthday came at last,
696All its auguries fulfilling
697(For the presages of evil
698Seldom fail or even linger):
699Came with such a horoscope,
700That the sun rushed blood-red tinted
701Into a terrific combat
702With the dark moon that resisted;
703Earth its mighty lists outspread
704As with lessening lights diminished
705Strove the twin-lamps of the sky.
706'Twas of all the sun's eclipses
707The most dreadful that it suffered
708Since the hour its bloody visage
709Wept the awful death of Christ.
710For o'erwhelmed in glowing cinders
711The great orb appeared to suffer
712Nature's final paroxysm.
713Gloom the glowing noontide darkened,
714Earthquake shook the mightiest buildings,
715Stones the angry clouds rained down,
716And with blood ran red the rivers.
717In this frenzy of the sun,
718In its madness and delirium,
719Sigismund was born, thus early
720Giving proofs of his condition,
721Since his birth his mother slew,
722Just as if these words had killed her,
723"I am a man, since good with evil
724I repay here from the beginning,"—
725I, applying to my studies,
726Saw in them as 'twere forewritten
727This, that Sigismund would be
728The most cruel of all princes,
729Of all men the most audacious,
730Of all monarchs the most wicked;
731That his kingdom through his means
732Would be broken and partitioned,
733The academy of the vices,
734And the high school of sedition;
735And that he himself, borne onward
736By his crimes' wild course resistless,
737Would even place his feet on me;
738For I saw myself down-stricken,
739Lying on the ground before him
740(To say this what shame it gives me!)
741While his feet on my white hairs
742As a carpet were imprinted.
743Who discredits threatened ill,
744Specially an ill previsioned
745By one's study, when self-love
746Makes it his peculiar business?—
747Thus then crediting the fates
748Which far off my science witnessed,
749All these fatal auguries
750Seen though dimly in the distance,
751I resolved to chain the monster
752That unhappily life was given to,
753To find out if yet the stars
754Owned the wise man's weird dominion.
755It was publicly proclaimed
756That the sad ill-omened infant
757Was stillborn. I then a tower
758Caused by forethought to be builded
759'Mid the rocks of these wild mountains
760Where the sunlight scarce can gild it,
761Its glad entrance being barred
762By these rude shafts obeliscal.
763All the laws of which you know,
764All the edicts that prohibit
765Anyone on pain of death
766That secluded part to visit
767Of the mountain, were occasioned
768By this cause, so long well hidden.
769There still lives Prince Sigismund,
770Miserable, poor, in prison.
771Him alone Clotaldo sees,
772Only tends to and speaks with him;
773He the sciences has taught him,
774He the Catholic religion
775Has imparted to him, being
776Of his miseries the sole witness.
777Here there are three things: the first
778I rate highest, since my wishes
779Are, O Poland, thee to save
780From the oppression, the affliction
781Of a tyrant King, because
782Of his country and his kingdom
783He were no benignant father
784Who to such a risk could give it.
785Secondly, the thought occurs
786That to take from mine own issue
787The plain right that every law
788Human and divine hath given him
789Is not Christian charity;
790For by no law am I bidden
791To prevent another proving,
792Say, a tyrant, or a villain,
793To be one myself: supposing
794Even my son should be so guilty,
795That he should not crimes commit
796I myself should first commit them.
797Then the third and last point is,
798That perhaps I erred in giving
799Too implicit a belief
800To the facts foreseen so dimly;
801For although his inclination
802Well might find its precipices,
803He might possibly escape them:
804For the fate the most fastidious,
805For the impulse the most powerful.
806Even the planets most malicious
807Only make free will incline,
808But can force not human wishes.
809And thus 'twist these different causes
810Vacillating and unfixed,
811I a remedy have thought of
812Which will with new wonder fill you.
813I to-morrow morning purpose,
814Without letting it be hinted
815That he is my son, and therefore
816Your true King, at once to fix him
817As King Sigismund (for the name
818Still he bears that first was given him)
819'Neath my canopy, on my throne,
820And in fine in my position,
821There to govern and command you,
822Where in dutiful submission
823You will swear to him allegiance.
824My resources thus are triple,
825As the causes of disquiet
826Were which I revealed this instant.
827The first is; that he being prudent,
828Careful, cautious and benignant,
829Falsifying the wild actions
830That of him had been predicted,
831You'll enjoy your natural prince,
832He who has so long been living
833Holding court amid these mountains,
834With the wild beasts for his circle.
835Then my next resource is this:
836If he, daring, wild, and wicked,
837Proudly runs with loosened rein
838O'er the broad plain of the vicious,
839I will have fulfilled the duty
840Of my natural love and pity;
841Then his righteous deposition
842Will but prove my royal firmness,
843Chastisement and not revenge
844Leading him once more to the prison.
845My third course is this: the Prince
846Being what my words have pictured,
847From the love I owe you, vassals,
848I will give you other princes
849Worthier of the crown and sceptre;
850Namely, my two sisters' children,
851Who their separate pretensions
852Having happily commingled
853By the holy bonds of marriage,
854Will then fill their fit position.
855This is what a king commands you,
856This is what a father bids you,
857This is what a sage entreats you,
858This is what an old man wishes;
859And as Seneca, the Spaniard,
860Says, a king for all his riches
861Is but slave of his Republic,
862This is what a slave petitions.

ASTOLFO.

863If on me devolves the answer,
864As being in this weighty business
865The most interested party,
866I, of all, express the opinion:—
867Let Prince Sigismund appear;
868He's thy son, that's all-sufficient.

ALL.

869Give to us our natural prince,
870We proclaim him king this instant!

BASILIUS.

871Vassals, from my heart I thank you
872For this deference to my wishes:—
873Go, conduct to their apartments
874These two columns of my kingdom,
875On tomorrow you shall see him.

ALL.

876Live, long live great King Basilius!

[Exeunt all, accompanying ESTRELLA and ASTOLFO; The King remains.]

SCENE VII.

CLOTALDO, ROSAURA, CLARIN, and BASILIUS.

CLOTALDO.

877May I speak to you, sire?

BASILIUS.

878Clotaldo,
879You are always welcome with me.

CLOTALDO.

880Although coming to your feet
881Shows how freely I'm admitted,
882Still, your majesty, this once,
883Fate as mournful as malicious
884Takes from privilege its due right,
885And from custom its permission.

BASILIUS.

886What has happened?

CLOTALDO.

887A misfortune,
888Sire, which has my heart afflicted
889At the moment when all joy
890Should have overflown and filled it.

BASILIUS.

891Pray proceed.

CLOTALDO.

892This handsome youth here,
893Inadvertently, or driven
894By his daring, pierced the tower,
895And the Prince discovered in it.
896Nay . . . .

BASILIUS.

897Clotaldo, be not troubled
898At this act, which if committed
899At another time had grieved me,
900But the secret so long hidden
901Having myself told, his knowledge
902Of the fact but matters little.
903See me presently, for I
904Much must speak upon this business,
905And for me you much must do
906For a part will be committed
907To you in the strangest drama
908That perhaps the world e'er witnessed.
909As for these, that you may know
910That I mean not your remissness
911To chastise, I grant their pardon.

[Exit.]

CLOTALDO.

912Myriad years to my lord be given!

SCENE VIII.

CLOTALDO, ROSAURA, and CLARIN.

CLOTALDO

913Heaven has sent a happier fate;aparte
914Since I need not now admit it,
915I'll not say he is my son. —
916Strangers who have wandered hither,
917You are free.

ROSAURA.

918I give your feet
919A thousand kisses.

CLARIN.

920I say misses,
921For a letter more or less
922'Twixt two friends is not considered.

ROSAURA.

923You have given me life, my lord,
924And since by your act I'm living,
925I eternally will own me
926As your slave.

CLOTALDO.

927The life I've given
928Is not really your true life,
929For a man by birth uplifted
930If he suffers an affront
931Actually no longer liveth;
932And supposing you have come here
933For revenge as you have hinted,
934I have not then given you life,
935Since you have not brought it with you,
936For no life disgraced is life.—
937[Aside.] (This I say to arouse his spirit.)aparte

ROSAURA.

938I confess I have it not,
939Though by you it has been given me;
940But revenge being wreaked, my honour
941I will leave so pure and limpid,
942All its perils overcome,
943That my life may then with fitness
944Seem to be a gift of yours.

CLOTALDO.

945Take this burnished sword which hither
946You brought with you; for I know,
947To revenge you, 'tis sufficient,
948In your enemy's blood bathed red;
949For a sword that once was girded
950Round me (I say this the while
951That to me it was committed),
952Will know how to right you.

ROSAURA.

953Thus
954In your name once more I gird it,
955And on it my vengeance swear,
956Though the enemy who afflicts me
957Were more powerful.

CLOTALDO.

958Is he so?

ROSAURA.

959Yes; so powerful, I am hindered
960Saying who he is, not doubting
961Even for greater things your wisdom
962And calm prudence, but through fear
963Lest against me your prized pity
964Might be turned.

CLOTALDO.

965'Twill rather be,
966By declaring it, more kindled;
967Otherwise you bar the passage
968'Gainst your foe of my assistance.—
969[Aside.] (Would that I but knew his name!)aparte

ROSAURA.

970Not to think I set so little
971Value on such confidence,
972Know my enemy and my victim
973Is no less than Prince Astolfo,
974Duke of Muscovy.

CLOTALDO

975[aside]. Resistanceaparte
976Badly can my grief supply
977Since 'tis heavier than I figured.
978Let us sift the matter deeper. —
979If a Muscovite by birth, then
980He who is your natural lord
981Could not 'gainst you have committed
982Any wrong; reseek your country,
983And abandon the wild impulse
984That has driven you here.

ROSAURA.

985I know,
986Though a prince, he has committed
987'Gainst me a great wrong.

CLOTALDO.

988He could not,
989Even although your face was stricken
990By his angry hand. [Aside.] (Oh, heavens!)aparte

ROSAURA.

991Mine's a wrong more deep and bitter.

CLOTALDO.

992Tell it, then; it cannot be
993Worse than what my fancy pictures.

ROSAURA.

994I will tell it; though I know not,
995With the respect your presence gives me,
996With the affection you awaken,
997With the esteem your worth elicits,
998How with bold face here to tell you
999That this outer dress is simply
1000An enigma, since it is not
1001What it seems. And from this hint, then,
1002If I'm not what I appear,
1003And Astolfo with this princess
1004Comes to wed, judge how by him
1005I was wronged: I've said sufficient.

[Exeunt ROSAURA and CLARIN.]

CLOTALDO.

1006Listen! hear me! wait! oh, stay!
1007What a labyrinthine thicket
1008Is all this, where reason gives
1009Not a thread whereby to issue?
1010My own honour here is wronged,
1011Powerful is my foe's position,
1012I a vassal, she a woman;
1013Heaven reveal some way in pity,
1014Though I doubt it has the power;
1015When in such confused abysses,
1016Heaven is all one fearful presage,
1017And the world itself a riddle.

Act II

A HALL IN THE ROYAL PALACE.

SCENE I.

BASILIUS and CLOTALDO.

CLOTALDO.

1018Everything has been effected
1019As you ordered.

BASILIUS.

1020How all happened
1021Let me know, my good Clotaldo.

CLOTALDO.

1022It was done, sire, in this manner.
1023With the tranquillising draught,
1024Which was made, as you commanded,
1025Of confections duly mixed
1026With some herbs, whose juice extracted
1027Has a strange tyrannic power,
1028Has some secret force imparted,
1029Which all human sense and speech
1030Robs, deprives, and counteracteth,
1031And as 'twere a living corpse
1032leaves the man whose lips have quaffed it
1033So asleep that all his senses,
1034All his powers are overmastered . . . .
1035— No need have we to discuss
1036That this fact can really happen,
1037Since, my lord, experience gives us
1038Many a clear and proved example;
1039Certain 'tis that Nature's secrets
1040May by medicine be extracted,
1041And that not an animal,
1042Not a stone, or herb that's planted,
1043But some special quality
1044Doth possess: for if the malice
1045Of man's heart, a thousand poisons
1046That give death, hath power to examine,
1047Is it then so great a wonder
1048That, their venom being abstracted,
1049If, as death by some is given,
1050Sleep by others is imparted?
1051Putting, then, aside the doubt
1052That 'tis possible this should happen,
1053A thing proved beyond all question
1054Both by reason and example . . . .
1055— With the sleeping draught, in fine,
1056Made of opium superadded
1057To the poppy and the henbane,
1058I to Sigismund's apartment —
1059Cell, in fact — went down, and with him
1060Spoke awhile upon the grammar
1061Of the sciences, those first studies
1062Which mute Nature's gentle masters,
1063Silent skies and hills, had taught him;
1064In which school divine and ample,
1065The bird's song, the wild beast's roar,
1066Were a lesson and a language.
1067Then to raise his spirit more
1068To the high design you planned here,
1069I discoursed on, as my theme,
1070The swift flight, the stare undazzled
1071Of a pride-plumed eagle bold,
1072Which with back-averted talons,
1073Scorning the tame fields of air,
1074Seeks the sphere of fire, and passes
1075Through its flame a flash of feathers,
1076Or a comet's hair untangled.
1077I extolled its soaring flight,
1078Saying, "Thou at last art master
1079Of thy house, thou'rt king of birds,
1080It is right thou should'st surpass them."
1081He who needed nothing more
1082Than to touch upon the matter
1083Of high royalty, with a bearing
1084As became him, boldly answered;
1085For in truth his princely blood
1086Moves, excites, inflames his ardour
1087To attempt great things: he said,
1088"In the restless realm of atoms
1089Given to birds, that even one
1090Should swear fealty as a vassal!
1091I, reflecting upon this,
1092Am consoled by my disasters,
1093For, at least, if I obey,
1094I obey through force: untrammelled,
1095Free to act, I ne'er will own
1096Any man on earth my master."—
1097This, his usual theme of grief,
1098Having roused him nigh to madness,
1099I occasion took to proffer
1100The drugged draught: he drank, but hardly
1101Had the liquor from the vessel
1102Passed into his breast, when fastest
1103Sleep his senses seized, a sweat,
1104Cold as ice, the life-blood hardened
1105In his veins, his limbs grew stiff,
1106So that, knew I not 'twas acted,
1107Death was there, feigned death, his life
1108I could doubt not had departed.
1109Then those, to whose care you trust
1110This experiment, in a carriage
1111Brought him here, where all things fitting
1112The high majesty and the grandeur
1113Of his person are provided.
1114In the bed of your state chamber
1115They have placed him, where the stupor
1116Having spent its force and vanished,
1117They, as 'twere yourself, my lord,
1118Him will serve as you commanded:
1119And if my obedient service
1120Seems to merit some slight largess,
1121I would ask but this alone
1122(My presumption you will pardon),
1123That you tell me, with what object
1124Have you, in this secret manner,
1125To your palace brought him here?

BASILIUS.

1126Good Clotaldo, what you ask me
1127Is so just, to you alone
1128I would give full satisfaction.
1129Sigismund, my son, the hard
1130Influence of his hostile planet
1131(As you know) doth threat a thousand
1132Dreadful tragedies and disasters;
1133I desire to test if Heaven
1134(An impossible thing to happen)
1135Could have lied — if having given us
1136Proofs unnumbered, countless samples
1137Of his evil disposition,
1138He might prove more mild, more guarded
1139At the lest, and self-subdued
1140By his prudence and true valour
1141Change his character; for 'tis man
1142That alone controls the planets.
1143This it is I wish to test,
1144Having brought him to this palace,
1145Where he'll learn he is my son,
1146And display his natural talents.
1147If he nobly hath subdued him,
1148He will reign; but if his manners
1149Show him tyrannous and cruel,
1150Then his chains once more shall clasp him.
1151But for this experiment,
1152Now you probably will ask me
1153Of what moment was't to bring him
1154Thus asleep and in this manner?
1155And I wish to satisfy you,
1156Giving all your doubts an answer.
1157If to-day he learns that he
1158Is my son, and some hours after
1159Finds himself once more restored
1160To his misery and his shackles,
1161Certain 'tis that from his temper
1162Blank despair may end in madness —
1163But once knowing who he is,
1164Can he be consoled thereafter?
1165Yes, and thus I wish to leave
1166One door open, one free passage,
1167By declaring all he saw
1168Was a dream. With this advantage
1169We attain two ends. The first
1170Is to put beyond all cavil
1171His condition, for on waking
1172He will show his thoughts, his fancies:
1173To console him is the second;
1174Since, although obeyed and flattered,
1175He beholds himself awhile,
1176And then back in prison shackled
1177Finds him, he will think he dreamed.
1178And he rightly so may fancy,
1179For, Clotaldo, in this world
1180All who live but dream they act here.

CLOTALDO.

1181Reasons fail me not to show
1182That the experiment may not answer;
1183But there is no remedy now,
1184For a sign from the apartment
1185Tells me that he hath awoken
1186And even hitherward advances.

BASILIUS.

1187It is best that I retire;
1188But do you, so long his master,
1189Near him stand; the wild confusion
1190That his waking sense may darken
1191Dissipate by simple truth.

CLOTALDO.

1192Then your licence you have granted
1193That I may declare it?

BASILIUS.

1194Yes;
1195For it possibly may happen
1196That admonished of his danger
1197He may conquer his worst passions.

[Exit]

SCENE II.

CLARIN and CLOTALDO.

CLARIN.

1198[aside]. Four good blows are all it cost meaparte
1199To come here, inflicted smartly
1200By a red-robed halberdier,
1201With a beard to match his jacket,
1202At that price I see the show,
1203For no window's half so handy
1204As that which, without entreating
1205Tickets of the ticket-master,
1206A man carried with himself;
1207Since for all the feasts and galas
1208Cool effrontery is the window
1209Whence at ease he gazes at them.

CLOTALDO.

1210[aside]. This is Clarin, heavens! of her,aparte
1211Yes, I say, of her the valet,
1212She, who dealing in misfortunes,
1213Has my pain to Poland carried: —
1214Any news, friend Clarin?

CLARIN.

1215News?
1216Yes, sir, since your great compassion
1217Is disposed Rosaura's outrage
1218To revenge, she has changed her habit,
1219And resumed her proper dress.

CLOTALDO.

1220'Tis quite right, lest possible scandal
1221Might arise.

CLARIN.

1222More news: her name
1223Having changed and wisely bartered
1224For your niece's name, she now
1225So in honour has advanced her,
1226That among Estrella's ladies
1227She here with her in the palace
1228Lives.

CLOTALDO.

1229'Tis right that I once more
1230Should her honour re-establish.

CLARIN.

1231News; that anxiously she waiteth
1232For that very thing to happen,
1233When you may have time to try it.

CLOTALDO.

1234Most discreetly has she acted;
1235Soon the time will come, believe me,
1236Happily to end this matter.

CLARIN.

1237News, too; that she's well regaled,
1238Feasted like a queen, and flattered
1239On the strength of being your niece.
1240And the last news, and the saddest,
1241Is that I who here came with her
1242Am with hunger almost famished.
1243None remember me, or think
1244I am Clarin, clarion rather,
1245And that if that clarion sounded,
1246All the Court would know what passes.
1247For there are two things, to wit,
1248A brass clarion and a lackey,
1249That are bad at keeping secrets;
1250And it so may chance, if haply
1251I am forced to break my silence,
1252They of me may sing this passage:
1253"Never, when the day is near,
1254Does clarion sound more clear."

CLOTALDO.

1255Your complaint is too well-founded;
1256I will get you satisfaction,
1257Meanwhile you may wait on me.

CLARIN.

1258See, sir, Sigismund advances.

SCENE III.

[Music and song.] SIGISMUND enters, lost in amazement. Servants minister to him, presenting costly robes. —CLOTALDO, and CLARIN.

SIGISMUND.

1259Help me, Heaven, what's this I see!
1260Help me, Heaven, what's this I view!
1261Things I scarce believe are true,
1262But, if true, which fright not me.
1263I in palaces of state?
1264I 'neath silks and cloth of gold?
1265I, around me, to behold
1266Rich-robed servants watch and wait?
1267I so soft a bed to press
1268While sweet sleep my senses bowed?
1269I to wake in such a crowd,
1270Who assist me even to dress?
1271'Twere deceit to say I dream,
1272Waking I recall my lot,
1273I am Sigismund, am I not?
1274Heaven make plain what dark doth seem!
1275Tell me, what has phantasy —
1276Wild, misleading, dream-adept —
1277So effected while I slept,
1278That I still the phantoms see?
1279But let that be as it may,
1280Why perplex myself and brood?
1281Better taste the present good,
1282Come what will some other day.

FIRST SERVANT.

1283[aside to the Second Servant, and to CLARIN]. What a sadness doth oppress him!aparte

SECOND SERVANT.

1284Who in such-like case would be
1285Less surprised and sad than he?

CLARIN.

1286I for one.

SECOND SERVANT.

1287[to the First]. You had best address him.

FIRST SERVANT.

1288[to SIGISMUND]. May they sing again?

SIGISMUND.

1289No, no;
1290I don't care to hear them sing.

SECOND SERVANT.

1291I conceived the song might bring
1292To your thought some ease.

SIGISMUND.

1293Not so;
1294Voiced that but charm the ear
1295Cannot soothe my sorrow's pain;
1296'Tis the soldier's martial strain
1297That alone I love to hear.

CLOTALDO.

1298May your Highness, mighty Prince,
1299Deign to let me kiss your hand,
1300I would first of all this land
1301My profound respect evince.

SIGISMUND.

1302[aside]. 'Tis my gaoler! how can heaparte
1303Change his harshness and neglect
1304To this language of respect?
1305What can have occurred to me?

CLOTALDO.

1306The new state in which I find you
1307Must create a vague surprise,
1308Doubts unnumbered must arise
1309To bewilder and to blind you;
1310I would make your prospect fair,
1311Through the maze a path would show,
1312Thus, my lord, 'tis right you know
1313That you are the prince and heir
1314Of this Polish realm: if late
1315You lay hidden and concealed
1316'Twas that we were forced to yield
1317To the stern decrees of fate,
1318Which strange ills, I know not how,
1319Threatened on this land to bring
1320Should the laurel of a king
1321Ever crown thy princely brow.
1322Still relying on the power
1323Of your will the stars to bind,
1324For a man of resolute mind
1325Can them bind how dark they lower;
1326To this palace from your cell
1327In your life-long turret keep
1328They have borne you while dull sleep
1329Held your spirit in its spell.
1330Soon to see you and embrace
1331Comes the King, your father, here —
1332He will make the rest all clear.

SIGISMUND.

1333Why, thou traitor vile and base,
1334What need I to know the rest,
1335Since it is enough to know
1336Who I am my power to show,
1337And the pride that fills my breast?
1338Why this treason brought to light
1339Has thou to thy country done,
1340As to hide from the King's son,
1341'Gainst all reason and all right,
1342This his rank?

CLOTALDO.

1343Oh, destiny!

SIGISMUND.

1344Thou the traitor's part has played
1345'Gainst the law; the King betrayed,
1346And done cruel wrong to me;
1347Thus for each distinct offence
1348Have the law, the King, and I
1349Thee condemned this day to die
1350By my hands.

SECOND SERVANT.

1351Prince . . . .

SIGISMUND.

1352No pretence
1353Shall undo the debt I owe you.
1354Catiff, hence! By Heaven! I say,
1355If you dare to stop my way
1356From the window I will throw you.

SECOND SERVANT.

1357Fly, Clotaldo!

CLOTALDO.

1358Woe to thee,
1359In thy pride so powerful seeming,
1360Without knowing thou art dreaming!

[Exit.]

SECOND SERVANT.

1361Think . . . .

SIGISMUND.

1362Away! don't trouble me.

SECOND SERVANT.

1363He could not the King deny.

SIGISMUND.

1364Bade to do a wrongful thing
1365He should have refused the King;
1366And, besides, his prince was I.

SECOND SERVANT.

1367'Twas not his affair to try
1368If the act was wrong or right.

SIGISMUND.

1369You're indifferent, black or white,
1370Since so pertly you reply.

CLARIN.

1371What the Prince says is quite true,
1372What you do is wrong, I say.

SECOND SERVANT.

1373Who gave you this licence, pray?

CLARIN.

1374No one gave; I took it.

SIGISMUND.

1375Who
1376Art thou, speak?

CLARIN.

1377A meddling fellow,
1378Prating, prying, fond of scrapes,
1379General of all jackanapes,
1380And most merry when most mellow.

SIGISMUND.

1381You alone in this new sphere

BASILIUS.

1493What's all this?

SIGISMUND.

1575Still untamed and uncontrolled;—

SIGISMUND.

1587Is this, then, a phantom scene? —

ROSAURA.

1886Would I knew it not! O help me

1899From my earliest misfortune
