2547Slight help there is for what is fixed by fate,
2548And much of danger to foresee the blow;
2549If it must fall, defence is then too late,
2550And he who most forestalls doth most foreknow.
2551Hard law! Stern rule! Dire fact to contemplate!
2552That he who thinks to fly doth nearer go.
2553Thus by the very means that I employed,
2554My country and myself I have destroyed.

SCENE VI.

ESTRELLA and BASILIUS.

ESTRELLA.

2555If, mighty lord, thy presence, which it braves,
2556The tumult of the crowd cannot defeat —
2557The frenzy of the multitude that raves
2558In hostile bands through every square and street,—
2559Thou'lt see thy kingdom swim in crimson waves,
2560A purple sea of blood shall round it beat;
2561For even already in its dismal doom
2562All is disaster, tragedy, and gloom.
2563Such is thy kingdom's ruin, so severe
2564The hard and bloody trial fate hath sent,
2565Dazed is the eye, and terrified the ear;
2566Dark grows the sun, and every wind is spent;
2567Each stone a mournful obelisk doth rear,
2568And every flower erects a monument;
2569A grave seems every house, whence life is gone,—
2570Each soldier is a living skeleton.

SCENE VII.

CLOTALDO, BASILIUS, and ESTRELLA.

CLOTALDO.

2571Thanks be to God, I reach thy feet alive.

BASILIUS.

2572What news of Sigismund, Clotaldo, say?

CLOTALDO.

2573The crowd, whom frenzy and blind impulse drive,
2574Into the tower resistless burst their way,
2575Released the Prince, who seeing thus revive
2576The honour he had tasted for one day,
2577Looked brave, declaring, in a haughty tone,
2578The truth at last that heaven must now make known.

BASILIUS.

2579Give me a horse! In person forth I'll ride
2580To check the pride of this ungrateful son.
2581Where Science erred let now the sword decide;
2582By my own valour shall my throne be won!

[Exit.

ESTRELLA.

2583Let me the glory of the fight divide —
2584A twinkling star beside that royal sun —
2585Bellona matched with Mars: for I would dare
2586To scale even heaven to rival Pallas there.

[Exit, and they sound to arms.

SCENE VIII.

ROSAURA, who detains CLOTALDO.

ROSAURA.

2587Though the trumpets from afar
2588Echo in thy valorous breast,
2589Hear me, list to my request,
2590For I know that all is war.
2591Well thou knowest that I came
2592Poor to Poland, sad, dejected;
2593And that graciously protected,
2594Thou thy pity let me claim.
2595It was thy command, ah, me!
2596I should live here thus disguised,
2597Striving, as thy words advised
2598(Hiding all my jealousy),
2599To avoid Astolfo's sight;
2600But he saw me, and though seeing,
2601With Estrella, he — false being!—
2602Converse holds this very night
2603In a garden bower. The key
2604I have taken, and will show
2605Where, by entering, with a blow
2606Thou canst end my misery.
2607Thus, then, daring, bold, and strong,
2608Thou my honour wilt restore;
2609Strike, and hesitate no more,
2610Let his death revenge my wrong.

CLOTALDO.

2611It is true, my inclination
2612Since thou first wert seen by me,
2613Was to strive and do for thee
2614(Be thy tears my attestation)
2615All my life could do to serve thee.
2616What I first was forced to press,
2617Was that thou should'st change thy dress;
2618Les if chancing to observe thee
2619Masquerading like a page,
2620By appearances so strong
2621Led astray, the Duke might wrong
2622By a thought thy sex and age.
2623Meanwhile various projects held me
2624In suspense, oft pondering o'er
2625How thy honour to restore;
2626Though (thy honour so compelled me)
2627I Astolfo's life should take —
2628Wild design that soon took wing —
2629Yet, as he was not my king,
2630It no terror could awake.
2631I his death was seeking, when
2632Sigismund with vengeful aim
2633Sought for mine; Astolfo came,
2634And despising what most men
2635Would a desperate peril deem,
2636Stood in my defence; his bearing,
2637Nigh to rashness in its daring,
2638Showed a valour most extreme.
2639How then, think, could I, whose breath
2640Is his gift, in murderous strife,
2641For his giving me my life,
2642Strive in turn to give him death?
2643And thus, grateful, yet aggrieved,
2644By two opposite feelings driven,
2645Seeing it to thee have given,
2646And from him have it received,
2647Doubting this, and that believing,
2648Half revenging, half forgiving,
2649If to thee I'm drawn by giving,
2650I to him am by receiving;
2651Thus bewildered and beset,
2652Vainly seeks my love a way,
2653Since I have a debt to pay,
2654Where I must exact a debt

ROSAURA.

2655It is settled, I believe,
2656As all men of spirit know,
2657That 'tis glorious to bestow,
2658But a meanness to receive.
2659Well, admitting this to be,
2660Then thy thanks should not be his,
2661Even supposing that he is
2662One who gave thy life to thee;
2663As the gift of life was thine,
2664And from him the taking came,
2665In this case the act was shame,
2666And a glorious act in mine.
2667Thus by him thou art aggrieved,
2668And by me even complimented,
2669Since to me thou hast presented
2670What from him thou hast received:
2671Then all hesitation leaving,
2672Thou to guard my fame shouldst fly,
2673Since my honour is as high
2674As is giving to receiving.

CLOTALDO.

2675Thou it seems a generous fever
2676In a noble heart to give,
2677Still an equal fire may live
2678In the heart of the receiver.
2679Heartlessness is something hateful,
2680I would boast a liberal name;
2681Thus I put my highest claim
2682In the fact of being grateful.
2683Then to me that title leave,—
2684Gentle birth breeds gentleness;
2685For the honour is no less
2686To bestow than to receive.

ROSAURA.

2687I received my life from thee,
2688But for thee I now were dead;
2689Still it was thyself that said
2690No insulted life could be
2691Called a life: on that I stand;
2692Nought have I received from thee,
2693For the life no life could be
2694That was given me by thy hand.
2695But if thou wouldst first be just
2696Ere being generous in this way
2697(As I heard thyself once say),
2698Thou will give me life I trust,
2699Which thou hast not yet; and thus
2700Giving will enhance thee more,
2701For if liberal before,
2702Thou wilt then be generous.

CLOTALDO.

2703Conquered by thy argument,
2704Liberal I first will be.
2705I, Rosaura, will to thee
2706All my property present;
2707In a convent live; by me
2708Has the plan been weighed some time,
2709For escaping from a crime
2710Thou wilt there find sanctuary;
2711For so many ills present them
2712Through the land on every side,
2713That being nobly born, my pride
2714Is to strive and not augment them.
2715By the choice that I have made,
2716Loyal to the land I'll be,
2717I am liberal with thee,
2718And Astolfo's debt is paid;
2719Choose then, nay, let honour, rather,
2720Choose for thee, and for us two,
2721For, by Heaven! I could not do
2722More for thee were I thy father!—

ROSAURA.

2723Were that supposition true,
2724I might strive and bear this blow;
2725But not being my father, no.

CLOTALDO.

2726What then dost thou mean to do?

ROSAURA.

2727Kill the Duke.

CLOTALDO.

2728A gentle dame,
2729Who no father's name doth know,
2730Can she so much valour show?

ROSAURA.

2731Yes.

CLOTALDO.

2732What drives thee on?

ROSAURA.

2733My fame.

CLOTALDO.

2734Think that in the Duke thou'lt see . . . .

ROSAURA.

2735Honour all my wrath doth rouse.

CLOTALDO.

2736Soon thy king — Estrella's spouse.

ROSAURA.

2737No, by Heaven! it must not be.

CLOTALDO.

2738It is madness.

ROSAURA.

2739Yes, I see it.

CLOTALDO.

2740Conquer it.

ROSAURA.

2741I can't o'erthrow it.

CLOTALDO.

2742It will cost thee . . . .

ROSAURA.

2743Yes, I know it.

CLOTALDO.

2744Life and honour.

ROSAURA.

2745Well, so be it.

CLOTALDO.

2746What wouldst have?

ROSAURA.

2747My death.

CLOTALDO.

2748Take care!
2749It is spite.

ROSAURA.

2750'Tis honour's cure.

CLOTALDO.

2751'Tis wild fire.

ROSAURA.

2752That will endure.

CLOTALDO.

2753It is frenzy.

ROSAURA.

2754Rage, despair.

CLOTALDO.

2755Can there then be nothing done
2756This blind rage to let pass by?

ROSAURA.

2757No.

CLOTALDO.

2758And who will help thee?

ROSAURA.

2759I.

CLOTALDO.

2760Is there then no remedy?

ROSAURA.

2761None.

CLOTALDO.

2762Think of other means whereby . . . .

ROSAURA.

2763Other means would seal my fate.

[Exit.

CLOTALDO.

2764If 'tis so, then, daughter, wait,
2765For together we shall die.

[Exit.

SCENE IX.

THE OPEN PLAIN.

SIGISMUND, clothed in skins: Soldiers marching. CLARIN.

[Drums are heard.]

SIGISMUND.

2766If Rome could see me on this day
2767Amid the triumphs of its early sway,
2768Oh, with what strange delight
2769It would have seen so singular a sight,
2770Its mighty armies led
2771By one who was a savage wild beast bred,
2772Whose courage soars so high,
2773That even an easy conquest seems the sky!
2774But let us lower our flight,
2775My spirit; 'tis not thus we should invite
2776This doubtful dream to stay,
2777Lest when I wake and it has past away,
2778I learn to my sad cost,
2779A moment given, 'twas in a moment lost;
2780Determined not to abuse it,
2781The less will be my sorrow should I lose it.

[A trumpet sounds.

CLARIN.

2782Upon a rapid steed,
2783(Excuse my painting it; I can't indeed
2784Resist the inspiration),
2785Which seems a moving mass of all creation,
2786Its body being the earth,
2787The fire the soul that in its heart hath birth,
2788Its foam the sea, its panting breath the air,
2789Chaos confused at which I stand and stare,
2790Since in its soul, foam, body, breath, to me
2791It is a monster made of fire, earth, air, and sea;
2792Its colour dapple grey,
2793Speckled its skin, and flecked, as well it may,
2794By the impatient spur its flank that dyes,
2795For lo! it doth not run, the meteor flies;
2796As borne upon the wind,
2797A beauteous woman seeks thee.

SIGISMUND.

2798I'm struck blind!

CLARIN.

2799Good God, it is Rosaura, oh, the pain!

[Retires.

SIGISMUND.

2800Heaven has restored her to my sight again.

SCENE X.

ROSAURA, in a light corselet, with sword and dagger;

SIGISMUND, and Soldiers.

ROSAURA.

2801Noble-hearted Sigismund!
2802Thou whose hidden light heroic
2803Issues from its night of shadows
2804To the great deeds of its morning;
2805And as heaven's sublimest planet
2806From the white arms of Aurora
2807Back restores their beauteous colour
2808To the wild flowers and the roses,
2809And upon the seas and mountains,
2810When endiademed with glory,
2811Scatters light, diffuses splendour,
2812Braids their foam, their hair makes golden;
2813Thus thou dawnest on the world
2814Bright auspicious sun of Poland,
2815Who will help a hapless woman,
2816She who at thy feet doth throw her,
2817Help her, since she is unhappy,
2818And a woman; two good motives
2819Quite enough to move a man
2820Who of valour so doth boast him,
2821Though even one would be sufficient,
2822Though even one would be all potent.
2823Thou hast seen me thrice already,
2824Thrice thou hast not truly known me,
2825For each time by different dresses
2826Was I strangely metamorphosed.
2827First I seemed to thee a man,
2828When within thy sad and sombre
2829Cell thou sawest me, when thy life
2830Wiled from me mine own misfortunes.
2831As a woman next thou sawest me,
2832Where the splendours of thy throne-room
2833Vanished like a fleeting vision,
2834Vain, phantasmal and abortive.
2835The third time is now, when being
2836Something monstrous and abnormal,
2837In a woman's dress thou see'st me
2838With a warrior's arms adorned.
2839And to pity and compassion
2840That thou may'st be moved more strongly,
2841Listen to the sad succession
2842Of my tragical misfortunes.
2843In the Court of Muscovy
2844I was born of a noble mother,
2845Who indeed must have been fair
2846Since unhappiness was her portion.
2847Fond and too persuading eyes
2848Fixed on her, a traitor lover,
2849Whom, not knowing, I don't name,
2850Though mine own worth hath informed me
2851What was his: for being his image,
2852I sometimes regret that fortune
2853Made me not a pagan born,
2854That I might, in my wild folly,
2855Think he must have been some god,
2856Such as he was, who in golden
2857Shower wooed Danae, or as swan
2858Leda loved, as bull, Europa.
2859When I thought to lengthen out,
2860Citing these perfidious stories,
2861My discourse, I find already
2862That I have succinctly told thee
2863How my mother, being persuaded
2864By the flatteries of love's homage,
2865Was a fair as any fair,
2866And unfortunate as all are.
2867That ridiculous excuse
2868Of a plighted husband's promise
2869So misled her, that even yet
2870the remembrance brings her sorrow.
2871For that traitor, that Aeneas
2872Flying from his Troy, forgot there,
2873Or left after him his sword.
2874By this sheath its blade is covered,
2875But it shall be naked drawn
2876Ere this history is over.
2877From this loosely fastened know
2878Which binds nothing, which ties nothing,
2879Call it marriage, call it crime,
2880Names its nature cannot alter,
2881I was born, a perfect image,
2882A true copy of my mother,
2883In her loveliness, ah, no!
2884In her miseries and misfortunes.
2885Therefore there is little need
2886To say how the hapless daughter,
2887Heiress of such scant good luck,
2888Had her own peculiar portion.
2889All that I will say to thee
2890Of myself is, that the robber
2891Of the trophies of my fame,
2892Of the sweet spoils of my honour,
2893Is Astolfo . . . . Ah! to name him
2894Stirs and rouses up the choler
2895Of the heart, a fitting effort
2896When an enemy's name is spoken,—
2897Yes, Astolfo was that traitor,
2898Who, forgetful of his promise
2899(For when love has passed away,
2900Even its memory is forgotten),
2901Came to Poland, hither called.
2902From so sweet so proud a conquest,
2903To be married to Estrella,
2904Of my setting sun the torch light.
2905Who'll believe that when one star
2906Oft unites two happy lovers,
2907Now one star, Estrella, comes
2908Two to tear from one another?
2909I offended, I deceived,
2910Sad remained, remained astonished,
2911Mad, half dead, remained myself;
2912That's to say, in so much torment,
2913That my heart was like a Babel
2914Of confusion, hell, and horror:
2915I resolving to be mute,
2916(For there are some pains and sorrows
2917That by feelings are expressed,
2918Better than when words are spoken).
2919I by silence spoke my pain,
2920Till one day being with my mother
2921Violante, she (oh, heavens!)
2922Burst their prison; like a torrent
2923Forth they rushed from out my breast,
2924Streaming wildly o'er each other.
2925No embarrassment it gave me
2926To relate them, for the knowing
2927That the person we confide to
2928A like weakness must acknowledge
2929Gives as 'twere to our confusion
2930A sweet soothing and a solace,
2931For at times a bad example
2932Has its use. In fine, my sorrows
2933She with pity heard, relating
2934Even her own grief to console me:
2935When he has himself been guilty
2936With what ease the judge condoneth!
2937Knowing from her own experience
2938That 'twas idle, to slow-moving
2939Leisure, to swift-fleeting time,
2940To intrust one's injured honour.
2941She could not advise me better,
2942As the cure of my misfortunes,
2943Than to follow and compel him
2944By prodigious acts of boldness
2945To repay my honour's debt:
2946And that such attempt might cost me
2947Less, my fortune wished that I
2948Should a man's strange dress put on me.
2949She took down an ancient sword,
2950Which is this I bear: the moment
2951Now draws nigh I must unsheath it,
2952Since to her I gave that promise,
2953When confiding in its marks,
2954Thus she said, "Depart to Poland,
2955And so manage that this steel
2956Shall be seen by the chief nobles
2957Of that land, for I have hope
2958That there may be one among them
2959Who may prove to thee a friend,
2960An adviser and consoler."
2961Well, in Poland I arrived;
2962It is useless to inform thee
2963What thou knowest already, how
2964A wild steed resistless bore me
2965To thy caverned tower, wherein
2966Thou with wonder didst behold me.
2967Let us pass too, how Clotaldo
2968Passionately my cause supported,
2969How he asked my life of the king
2970Who to him that boon accorded;
2971How discovering who I am
2972He persuaded me my proper
2973Dress to assume, and on Estrella
2974To attend as maid of honour,
2975So to thwart Astolfo's love
2976And prevent the marriage contract.
2977Let us, too, pass by, that here
2978thou didst once again behold me
2979In a woman's dress, my form
2980Waking thus a twofold wonder,
2981And approach the time, Clotaldo
2982Being convinced it was important
2983That should wed and reign together
2984Fair Estrella and Astolfo,
2985'Gainst my honour, me advised
2986To forego my rightful project.
2987But, O valiant Sigismund,
2988Seeing that the moment cometh
2989For thy vengeance, since heaven wishes
2990Thee to-day to burst the portals
2991Of thy narrow rustic cell,
2992Where so long immured, thy body
2993Was to feeling a wild beast,
2994Was to sufferance what the rock is,
2995And that 'gainst thy sire and country
2996Thou hast gallantly revolted,
2997And ta'en arms, I come to assist thee,
2998Intermingling the bright corselet
2999Of Minerva with the trappings
3000Of Diana, thus enrobing
3001Silken stuff and shining steel
3002In a rare but rich adornment.
3003On, then, on, undaunted champion!
3004To us both it is important
3005To prevent and bring to nought
3006This engagement and betrothal;
3007First to me, that he, my husband,
3008Should not falsely wed another,
3009Then to thee, that their two staffs
3010Being united, their joined forces
3011Should with overwhelming power
3012Leave our doubtful victory hopeless.
3013Woman, I come here to urge thee
3014To repair my injured honour,
3015And as man I come to rouse thee
3016Crown and sceptre to recover.
3017Woman I would wake thy pity
3018Since here at thy feet I throw me,
3019And as man, my sword and person
3020In thy service I devote thee.
3021But remember, if to-day
3022As a woman thou should'st court me,
3023I, as man, will give thee death
3024In the laudable upholding,
3025Of my honour, since I am
3026In this strife of love, this contest,
3027Woman my complaints to tell thee,
3028And a man to guard my honour.

SIGISMUND.

3029[aside]. Heavens! if it is true I dream,aparte
3030Memory then suspend thy office,
3031For 'tis vain to hope remembrance
3032Could retain so many objects.
3033Help me, God! or teach me how
3034All these numerous doubts to conquer,
3035Or to cease to think of any!—
3036Whoe'er tried such painful problems?
3037If 'twas but a dream, my grandeur,
3038How then is it, at this moment,
3039That this woman can refer me
3040To some facts that are notorious?
3041Then 'twas truth, and not a dream;
3042But if it was truth (another
3043And no less confusion,) how
3044Can my life be called in proper
3045Speech a dream? So like to dreams
3046Are then all the world's chief glories,
3047That the true are oft rejected
3048As the false, the false too often
3049Are mistaken for the true?
3050Is there then 'twixt one and the other
3051Such slight difference, that a question
3052May arise at any moment
3053Which is true or which is false?
3054Are the original and the copy
3055So alike, that which is which
3056Oft the doubtful mind must ponder?
3057If 'tis so, and if must vanish,
3058As the shades of night at morning,
3059All of majesty and power,
3060All of grandeur and of glory,
3061Let us learn at least to turn
3062To our profit the brief moment
3063That is given us, since our joy
3064Lasteth while our dream lasts only.
3065In my power Rosaura stands,
3066Thou, my heart, her charms adoreth,
3067Let us seize then the occasion;
3068Let love trample in its boldness
3069All the laws on which relying
3070She here at my feet has thrown her.
3071'Tis a dream; and since 'tis so,
3072Let us dream of joys, the sorrows
3073Will come soon enough hereafter.
3074But with mine own words just spoken,
3075Let me now confute myself!
3076If it is a dream that mocks me,
3077Who for human vanities
3078Would forego celestial glory?
3079What past bliss is not a dream?
3080Who has had his happy fortunes
3081Who hath said not to himself
3082As his memory ran o'er them,
3083"All I saw, beyond a doubt
3084Was a dream." If this exposeth
3085My delusion, if I know
3086That desire is but the glowing
3087Of a flame that turns to ashes
3088At the softest wind that bloweth;
3089Let us seek then the eternal,
3090The true fame that ne'er reposeth,
3091Where the bliss is not a dream,
3092Nor the crown a fleeting glory.
3093Without honour is Rosaura.
3094But it is a prince's province
3095To give honour, not to take it:
3096Then, by Heaven! it is her honour
3097That for her I must win back,
3098Ere this kingdom I can conquer.
3099Let us fly then this temptation.
3100[To the Soldiers. 'Tis too strong: To arms! March onward!
3101For to-day I must give battle,
3102Ere descending night, the golden
3103Sunbeams of expiring day
3104Buries in the dark green ocean.

ROSAURA.

3105Dost thou thus, my lord, withdraw thee?
3106What! without a word being spoken?
3107Does my pain deserve no pity?
3108Does my grief so little move thee?
3109Can it be, my lord, thou wilt not
3110Deign to hear, to look upon me?
3111Dost thou even avert thy face?

SIGISMUND.

3112Ah, Rosaura, 'tis thy honour
3113That requires this harshness now,
3114If my pity I would show thee.
3115Yes, my voice does not respond,
3116'Tis my honour that respondeth;
3117True I speak not, for I wish
3118That my actions should speak for me;
3119Thee I do not look on, no,
3120For, alas! it is of moment,
3121That he must not see thy beauty
3122Who is pledged to see thy honour.

[Exit followed by the Soldiers.

ROSAURA.

3123What enigmas, O ye skies!
3124After many a sigh and tear,
3125Thus in doubt to leave me here
3126With equivocal replies!

SCENE XI.

CLARIN and ROSAURA.

CLARIN.

3127Madam, is it visiting hour?

ROSAURA.

3128Welcome, Clarin, where have you been?

CLARIN.

3129Only four stout walls between
3130In an old enchanted tower;
3131Death was on the cards for me,
3132But amid the sudden strife
3133Ere the last trump came, my life
3134Won the trick and I got free.
3135I ne'er hoped to sound again.

ROSAURA.

3136Why?

CLARIN.

3137Because alone I know
3138Who you are: And this being so,
3139Learn, Clotaldo is . . . . . This strain
3140Puts me out.

[Drums are heard.

ROSAURA.

3141What can it be?

CLARIN.

3142From the citadel at hand,
3143Leagured round, an armed band
3144As to certain victory
3145Sallies forth with flags unfurled.

ROSAURA.

3146'Gainst Prince Sigismund! and I,
3147Coward that I am, not by
3148To surprise and awe the world,
3149When with so much cruelty
3150Each on each the two hosts spring!

[Exit.

SCENE XII.

CLARIN; and Soldiers within.

Voices of some.

3151Live, long live our victor King!

Voices of others.

3152Live, long live our liberty!

CLARIN.

3153Live, long live the two, I say!
3154Me it matters not a pin,
3155Which doth lose or which doth win,
3156If I can keep out of the way!—
3157So aside here I will go,
3158Acting like a prudent hero,
3159Even as the Emperor Nero
3160Took things coolly long ago.
3161Or if care I cannot shun,
3162Let it 'bout mine ownself be;
3163Yes, here hidden I can see
3164All the fighting and the fun;
3165What a cosy place I spy
3166Mid the rock there! so secure,
3167Death can't find me out I'm sure,
3168Then a fig for death I say!

[Conceals himself, drums beat and the sound of arms is heard.

SCENE XIII.

BASILIUS, CLOTALDO, ASTOLFO, flying. — CLARIN concealed.

BASILIUS.

3169Hapless king! disastrous reign!
3170Outraged father! guilty son!

CLOTALDO.

3171See thy vanquished forces run
3172In a panic o'er the plain!

ASTOLFO.

3173And the rebel conqueror's stay,
3174Proud, defiant.

BASILIUS.

3175'Tis decreed
3176Those are loyal who succeed,
3177Rebels those who lose the day.
3178Let us then, Clotaldo, flee,
3179Since the victory he hath won,
3180From a proud and cruel son.

[Shots are fired within, and CLARIN falls wounded from his hiding-place.

CLARIN.

3181Heaven protect me!

ASTOLFO.

3182Who can be
3183This last victim of the fight,
3184Who is struck down in the retreat,
3185Falls here bleeding at our feet?

CLARIN.

3186I am an unlucky wight,
3187Who to shun Death's fearful face
3188Found the thing I would forget:
3189Flying from him, him I've met.
3190For there is no secret place
3191Hid from death; and therefore I
3192This conclusion hold as clear,
3193He 'scapes best who goes more near,
3194He dies first who first doth fly.
3195Then return, return and be
3196In the bloody conflict lost;
3197Where the battle rages most,
3198There is more security
3199Than in hills how desolate,
3200Since no safety can there be
3201'Gainst the force of destiny,
3202And the inclemency of fate;
3203Therefore 'tis in vain thou flyest
3204From the death thou draw'st more nigh,
3205Oh, take heed for thou must die
3206If it is God's will thou diest!

[Falls within.

BASILIUS.

3207Oh, take heed for thou must die
3208If it is God's will thou diest!—
3209With what eloquence, O heaven!
3210Does this body that here lieth,
3211Through the red mouth of a wound
3212To profoundest thoughts entice us
3213From our ignorance and our error!
3214The red current as it glideth
3215Is a bloody tongue that teaches
3216All man's diligence is idle,
3217When against a greater power,
3218And a higher cause it striveth.
3219Thus with me, 'gainst strife and murder
3220When I thought I had provided,
3221I but brought upon my country
3222All the ills I would have hindered.

CLOTALDO.

3223Though, my lord, fate knoweth well
3224Every path, and quickly findeth
3225Whom it seeks; yet still it strikes me
3226'Tis not christian-like to say
3227'Gainst its rage that nought suffices.
3228That is wrong, a prudent man
3229Even o'er fate victorious rises;
3230And if thou art not preserved
3231From the ills that have surprised thee,
3232From worse ills thyself preserve.

ASTOLFO.

3233Sire, Clotaldo doth address thee
3234As a cautious, prudent man,
3235Whose experience time hath ripened.
3236I as a bold youth would speak:
3237Yonder, having lost its rider,
3238I behold a noble steed
3239Wandering reinless and unbridled,
3240Mount and fly with him while I
3241Guard the open path behind thee.

BASILIUS.

3242If it is God's will I die,
3243Or if Death for me here lieth
3244As in ambush, face to face
3245I will meet it and defy it.

SCENE XIV.

SIGISMUND, ESTRELLA, ROSAURA, Soldiers, Attendants, BASILIUS,

ASTOLFO, and CLOTALDO.

A SOLDIER.

3246'Mid the thickets of the mountain,
3247'Neath these dark boughs so united,
3248The King hides.

SIGISMUND.

3249Pursue him then,
3250Leave no single shrub unrifled,
3251Nothing must escape your search,
3252Not a plant, and not a pine tree.

CLOTALDO.

3253Fly, my lord!

BASILIUS.

3254And wherefore fly?

ASTOLFO.

3255Come!

BASILIUS.

3256Astolfo, I'm decided.

CLOTALDO.

3257What to do?

BASILIUS.

3258To try, Clotaldo,
3259One sole remedy that surviveth.
3260[To SIGISMUND. If 'tis me thou'rt seeking, Prince,
3261At thy feet behold me lying.
3262[Kneeling. Let thy carpet be these hairs
3263Which the snows of age have whitened.
3264Tread upon my neck, and trample
3265On my crown; in base defilement
3266Treat me with all disrespect;
3267Let thy deadliest vengeance strike me
3268Through my honour; as thy slave
3269Make me serve thee, and in spite of
3270All precautions let fate be,
3271Let heaven keep the word it plighted.

SIGISMUND.

3272Princes of the Court of Poland,
3273Who such numerous surprises
3274Have astonished seen, attend,
3275For it is your prince invites ye.
3276That which heaven has once determined,
3277That which God's eternal finger
3278Has upon the azure tablets
3279Of the sky sublimely written,
3280Those transparent sheets of sapphire
3281Superscribed with golden ciphers
3282Ne'er deceive, and never lie;
3283The deceiver and the liar
3284Is he who to use them badly
3285In a wrongful sense defines them.
3286Thus, my father, who is present,
3287To protect him from the wildness
3288Of my nature, made of me
3289A fierce brute, a human wild-beast;
3290So that I, who from my birth,
3291From the noble blood that trickles
3292Through my veins, my generous nature,
3293And my liberal condition,
3294Might have proved a docile child,
3295And so grew, it was sufficient
3296By so strange an education,
3297By so wild a course of living,
3298To have made my manners wild;—
3299What a method to refine them!
3300If to any man 'twas said,
3301"It is fated that some wild-beast
3302will destroy you," would it be
3303Wise to wake a sleeping tiger
3304As the remedy of the ill?
3305If 'twere said, "this sword here hidden
3306In its sheath, which thou dost wear,
3307Is the one foredoomed to kill thee,"
3308Vain precaution it would be
3309To preserve the threatened victim.
3310Bare to point it at his breast.
3311If 'twere said, "these waves that ripple
3312Calmly here for thee will build
3313Foam-white sepulchres of silver,"
3314Wrong it were to trust the sea
3315When its haughty breast is lifted
3316Into mountain heights of snow,
3317Into hills of curling crystal.
3318Well, this very thing has happened
3319Unto him, who feared a wild-beast,
3320And awoke him while he slept;
3321Or who drew a sharp sword hidden
3322Naked forth, or dared the sea
3323When 'twas roused by raging whirlwinds
3324And though my fierce nature (hear me)
3325Was as 'twere the sleeping tiger,
3326A sheathed sword my innate rage
3327And my wrath a quiet ripple,
3328Fate should not be forced by means
3329So unjust and so vindictive,
3330For they but excite it more;
3331And thus he who would be victor
3332O'er his fortune, must succeed
3333By wise prudence and self-strictness.
3334Not before an evil cometh
3335Can it rightly be resisted
3336Even by him who hath foreseen it,
3337For although (the fact's admitted)
3338By an humble resignation
3339It is possible to diminish
3340Its effects, it first must happen,
3341And by no means can be hindered.
3342Let it serve as an example
3343This strange sight, this most surprising
3344Spectacle, this fear, this horror,
3345This great prodigy; for none higher
3346E'er was worked than this we see,
3347After years of vain contriving,
3348Prostrate at my feet a father,
3349And a mighty king submitted.
3350This the sentence of high heaven
3351Which he did his best to hinder
3352He could not prevent. Can I,
3353Who in valour and in science,
3354Who in years am so inferior,
3355It avert? My lord, forgive me,
3356[To the King. Rise, sir, let me clasp thy hand;
3357For since heaven has now apprized thee
3358That thy mode of counteracting
3359Its decree was wrong, a willing
3360Sacrifice to thy revenge
3361Let my prostrate neck be given.

BASILIUS.

3362Son, this noble act of thine
3363In my heart of hearts reviveth
3364All my love, thou'rt there reborn.
3365Thou art Prince; the bay that bindeth
3366Heroes' brows, the palm, be thine,
3367Let the crown thine own deeds give thee.

ALL.

3368Long live Sigismund our King!

SIGISMUND.

3369Though my sword must wait a little
3370Ere great victories it can gain,
3371I to-day will win the highest,
3372The most glorious, o'er myself.—
3373Give, Astolfo, give your plighted
3374Hand here to Rosaura, since
3375It is due and I require it.

ASTOLFO.

3376Though 'tis true I owe the debt,
3377Still 'tis needful to consider
3378That she knows not who she is;
3379It were infamous, a stigma
3380On my name to wed a woman . . . .

CLOTALDO.

3381Stay, Astolfo, do not finish;
3382For Rosaura is as noble
3383As yourself. My sword will right her
3384In the field against the world:
3385She's my daughter, that's sufficient.

ASTOLFO.

3386What do you say?

CLOTALDO.

3387Until I saw her
3388To a noble spouse united,
3389I her birth would not reveal.
3390It were now a long recital,
3391But the sum is, she's my child.

ASTOLFO.

3392That being so, the word I've plighted
3393I will keep.

SIGISMUND.

3394And that Estrella
3395May not now be left afflicted,
3396Seeing she has lost a prince
3397Of such valour and distinction,
3398I propose from mine own hand
3399As a husband one to give her,
3400Who, if he does not exceed
3401Him in worth, perhaps may rival.
3402Give to me thy hand.

ESTRELLA.

3403I gain
3404By an honour so distinguished.

SIGISMUND.

3405To Clotaldo, who so truly
3406Served my father, I can give him
3407But these open arms wherein
3408He will find what'er he wishes.

A SOLDIER.

3409If thou honorest those who serve thee,
3410Thus, to me the first beginner
3411Of the tumult through the land,
3412Who from out the tower, thy prison,
3413Drew thee forth, what wilt thou give?

SIGISMUND.

3414Just that tower: and that you issue
3415Never from it until death,
3416I will have you guarded strictly;
3417For the traitor is not needed
3418Once the treason is committed.

BASILIUS.

3419So much wisdom makes one wonder.

ASTOLFO.

3420What a change in his condition!

ROSAURA.

3421How discreet! how calm! how prudent!

SIGISMUND.

3422Why this wonder, these surprises,
3423If my teacher was a dream,
3424And amid my new aspirings
3425I am fearful I may wake,
3426And once more a prisoner find me
3427In my cell? But should I not,
3428Even to dream it is sufficient:
3429For I thus have come to know
3430That at last all human blisses
3431Pass and vanish as a dream,
3432And the time that may be given me
3433I henceforth would turn to gain:
3434Asking for our faults forgiveness,
3435Since to generous, noble hearts
3442It is natural to forgive them.
